findings.summary: Power is the set of conditions that let a business earn persistent returns above its cost of capital despite capable competitors. A strategy is a route to continuing Power in significant markets (the 'Mantra').
findings.limitations: Defined for shareholder value of a 'strategically separate business'; small owner-run firms often aim for owner income and stability, not differential returns above cost of capital.

findings.summary: Every Power needs a Benefit (higher price, lower cost or lower investment, and it must be material) and a Barrier (why rivals can't or won't compete it away). Benefits are common; Barriers are rare. Author's advice: examine the Barrier first.
findings.locator: text00006.html [152]-[162]; text00017.html [233]-[239] (3 S's: superior, significant, sustainable)
findings.limitations: Conceptual; no measurement method beyond stylized margin formulas.

findings.summary: Power is relative: assess it against each competitor separately, including potential and functional (substitute) competitors; one arbitrageur is enough to erase the margin. Assess each strategically separate business on its own.
findings.limitations: Requires competitor knowledge a small owner may not have.

findings.summary: Value is modelled as current market size x discounted growth x long-term share x long-term differential margin; summarised as potential value = market scale x Power. Operational excellence is needed to realise potential but is not itself Power.
findings.limitations: A valuation identity under simplifying assumptions; not a forecasting tool. Margin terms are long-run equilibria, not next quarter.

findings.summary: Scale Economies: unit cost falls as volume rises (fixed-cost spreading, volume/area, distribution density, learning, purchasing). Barrier: followers find share gains too costly because the leader can retaliate. Intensity needs both a material fixed cost relative to sales and a real scale lead; either term at zero means no Power.
findings.limitations: Stylized single-fixed-cost model; distribution density is the only listed source naturally bounded by geography.

findings.summary: Netflix converted content from a usage-priced input to a fixed cost via exclusives and originals, which made its subscriber lead a cost advantage; it first tested streaming with a small share of revenue before larger commitments.
findings.limitations: One large-company case viewed in hindsight by an investor in the company; not a template for small firms.

findings.summary: Network Economies: value to each user rises with the installed base. They tend to tip to one winner, are bounded by the network's real scope, and reward getting the early product right. Positive network effects can exist with no Power if the per-user network benefit times potential base cannot cover cost; often hard to size in advance.
findings.limitations: Linear homogeneous-benefit model is acknowledged as stylized.

findings.summary: BranchOut tried to build a professional network on Facebook's base, grew to millions of users, then collapsed when engagement and platform distribution failed; users wanted work and personal networks kept apart.
findings.limitations: Single venture-funded case; shows platform dependence risk as much as network theory.

findings.summary: Counter-Positioning: a newcomer adopts a superior business model that the incumbent rationally declines to copy because copying would damage its existing business (collateral damage). If the new model is unattractive on its own for the incumbent, it is not Counter-Positioning. Collateral damage comes from cannibalisation ('Milk'), incumbent cognitive bias, or managers' incentives.
findings.limitations: Built from large-incumbent cases (Vanguard/Fidelity, Netflix/Blockbuster, Kodak as a non-example).

findings.summary: Counter-Positioning only protects against the incumbent, not against other challengers using the same model; it is non-exclusive and therefore a partial strategy that needs another Power against like rivals. Collateral damage shrinks as the challenger grows and its model is proven, so incumbents eventually respond. The author suggests a challenger avoid trumpeting superiority, and notes very low early pricing can make the model look unattractive to the incumbent.
findings.limitations: Low or negative early margin is a tactic in a stylized single-period model, not tested guidance.

findings.summary: Switching Costs: the value a customer expects to lose by moving to another supplier for further purchases. Three types: financial, procedural (learning, risk of errors), relational (ties with staff, community, identity). Benefit exists only on follow-on sales to customers you already have.
findings.limitations: Typology cited from Burnham et al. 2003 (note 42).

findings.summary: Switching Costs are non-exclusive. As a market matures, every player can value an acquired customer, so competition for new customers bids away the Benefit; the main value comes from capturing customers before that happens. Add-on products extend and deepen switching costs.
findings.limitations: SAP case: large enterprise software; add-ons via acquisitions are not small-business options.

findings.summary: Branding: durable attribution of higher value to an objectively identical offer, from the seller's history. Benefit via good feelings or reduced uncertainty; Barrier is the long, uncertain build time (hysteresis). Pitfalls: dilution (e.g. going down-market), counterfeits, shifting tastes, geographic limits.
findings.limitations: Tiffany, Bayer, Halston examples are consumer luxury or pharma.

findings.summary: Branding as Power is narrower than marketing's 'brand': high awareness may really be Scale Economies (only big players can afford big ads). B2B goods rarely carry an emotional price premium; uncertainty-reduction branding suits categories with costly bad outcomes (safety, medicine, food, transport).
findings.limitations: Author's classification, not measured.

findings.summary: Cornered Resource: preferential access, on attractive terms, to a coveted asset that independently enhances value (talent group, patent, input rights). Barrier is 'fiat' (property, law, personal choice). Five screening tests: idiosyncratic, non-arbitraged (not paid away), transferable, ongoing, sufficient. Individual leaders usually fail the sufficiency test.
findings.limitations: Pixar Brain Trust argument is the author's interpretation from an investor's vantage.

findings.summary: Process Power: embedded organisation and activity sets giving lower cost or better product that rivals can match only with long commitment, because of complexity and tacit knowledge. It equals operational excellence plus a long time constant, and is rare. Operational excellence alone is copyable and is not strategy.
findings.limitations: Toyota/GM NUMMI case; author agrees with Porter that it is rare.

findings.summary: Experience-curve data cited from a 1990 study: about 60% of 108 cases had cost slopes of 70-85% per doubling of cumulative output; the author argues this shows shared improvement over time, not a position advantage.
findings.limitations: Manufacturing data from 1990; the histogram itself is missing from the EPUB.

findings.summary: All Power starts with invention (product, process, business model or brand); copying won't create Power. Invention also creates market size. Strategy is crafted through experimentation, not planned; most inventions do not yield Power.
findings.limitations: Drawn from venture-scale technology cases.

findings.summary: Compelling value has three paths with different risks: capabilities-led (need unknown; stay in the game, avoid big commitments), customer-led (need known; technical uncertainty), competitor-led (beat an existing product; big upfront commitments and complement deals, faster rival response).
findings.limitations: Adobe, Corning, Sony examples; the author rejects a fixed '10x' threshold.

findings.summary: Power Progression: Counter-Positioning and Cornered Resource are usually set in origination (before takeoff); Scale Economies, Network Economies and Switching Costs in takeoff; Process Power and Branding in stability. Each Barrier type has its own timing: collateral damage early, fiat before the resource is priced, cost of share gains only in takeoff, hysteresis only later.
findings.limitations: Charts missing; empirical support is a histogram of the author's students' papers (Fig 9.7, unreadable here).

findings.summary: Takeoff ends when business unit growth falls below roughly 30-40% a year (the author's experience-based cutoff). The stages are defined by business growth, not industry growth, and do not match product life-cycle stages.
findings.limitations: Heuristic for large markets; growth rates from a small base are noisy.

findings.summary: In takeoff customers ask 'can I get it?'; in stability they ask 'what is the best deal?', and each player prices share at its value, arbitraging it away. Strong financials during explosive growth are a common false positive for Power; arbitrage arrives when growth slows. In takeoff, execution and leadership can be decisive (Intel's sales push vs Apple III).
findings.limitations: Intel/Apple anecdotes.

findings.summary: The author reports concentrated personal equity returns 1994-2015 well above the S&P 500 using the framework, offered as evidence that Power is visible in advance.
findings.limitations: Self-reported, unaudited, single investor; says nothing about small-business growth decisions. Do not cite as evidence in plans.

findings.summary: The author claims the seven types are exhaustive in his and his students' cases (an empirical, not proven, claim) and that a business without at least one lacks a viable strategy. He says at any growth stage only up to three new Power types are worth exploring.
findings.limitations: 'No Power means no viable strategy' is framed for value creation in significant markets; read literally it misfits small owner-run businesses.

findings.summary: The authors reject the classic marketing funnel for recurring-revenue businesses because it ends at purchase, while those businesses depend on customers continuing to pay; marketing should not stop at signup.
findings.limitations: Argued for SaaS; little said about one-off purchase businesses.

findings.summary: Copying tactics from other companies is guessing; the needed information is the best customers' story from life before the product, through the trigger, search, choice, the value that convinced them to pay, and what changed after.
findings.limitations: Presented as a near-universal fix; the authors sell this method as consultants.

findings.summary: Authors report about 900% revenue growth at Unbounce and pre-revenue to $4M ARR at Calendly, each in two years on a seed round without paid acquisition.
findings.limitations: Self-reported by participants; no counterfactual; many other causes possible.

findings.summary: At Sprout Social, surveys and interviews showed agency customers wanted community and help growing their services, not revenue share; a beta with 100 agencies led to lower churn and $2.1M ARR in expansion within six months.
findings.limitations: Single company, reported outcome, no control.

findings.summary: Run the work with a small cross-functional team: a decision-maker who unblocks, a champion who drives, and consulted contributors (optional outside facilitator); adapt when roles are missing. Cites an HBR 2015 piece that most cross-functional teams are dysfunctional without a systematic approach.
findings.limitations: Organisational advice for 6-200 person firms; a solo owner plays all roles. HBR figure is a dated secondary citation.

findings.summary: Research participants should be the best customers: felt the problem, pay without hesitation, have an ongoing need, have clearly solved their problem with the product, and started paying recently enough to recall life before (ideally 3-6 months, up to a year).
findings.limitations: Deliberately excludes non-buyers, churned and struggling users.

findings.summary: Ask what happened, not opinions; use open-ended rather than leading, closed or multiple-choice questions so answers reveal the sequence and the customer's own words. The question set walks from current use back to the old way, the breaking-point moment, the search, discovery, choice, the moment of certainty, the new capability, and unmet wishes.
findings.limitations: Script is for recall of a successful purchase; recall bias not discussed.

findings.summary: Method rule of thumb: a best-customer pool of 500+ starts with a survey (assuming a 10-15% response rate) aiming for 25-50 high-quality responses; a smaller pool, or time for only one method, means 10-15 interviews.
findings.limitations: Authors' experience, no data; response rate depends on list, channel and relationship. Text says 'fewer than 500' for interviews while the table says '500 or fewer'.

findings.summary: Autobooks research showed one feature set (invoicing and card payments) drew customers; narrowing messaging to it and introducing other features one at a time at the point of need raised the signup rate after first exposure from 14% to 23% (reported +64%) and sustained card-payment customers by 300% within 30 days.
findings.limitations: Single case, 30-day window, consultants involved in the reported result.

findings.summary: Old research does not suffice: products, customers and markets change; demographic and product-usage data show who and what, not why.
findings.limitations: Repeat interval deferred to Ch9, which gives triggers not a schedule.

findings.summary: When there are no or too few best customers (new product, pivot), use audience research: target-market interviews, subscriber surveys, competitor review mining, audience tools and social listening. Results are hypotheses because respondents' fit is unknown.
findings.limitations: Methods listed, not specified; forum work called labour-intensive.

findings.summary: A website visitor survey captures people already in problem-solving mode: an awareness-stage question, their current tool, what they dislike about it, what matters most in a new solution, and what holds them back from signing up. Expect some junk answers; it can take weeks to collect enough depending on traffic.
findings.limitations: Survey best practices (conversion impact) are in the external workbook, not the book.

findings.summary: Paytouch launched a smaller online-ordering product (Dash) during COVID-19 from audience research and reports 980 restaurant customers; Tiller Money rewrote its homepage from website-survey answers and reports a 237% rise in Google Analytics page value.
findings.limitations: Page value is an attribution metric, not revenue; no control; pandemic context.

findings.summary: A Job is the struggle that motivated a customer to seek a desired outcome, written as a three-part 'when / help me / so I can' statement.
findings.limitations: Simplified JTBD; omits anxieties and habits (four forces) from the statement.

findings.summary: Parse research in four steps: tag each answer with struggle, motivation and outcome themes (several per quote allowed, one dimension at a time); count struggle themes; for each top struggle, filter to those respondents and find their most common motivations and outcomes; write 2-3 job statements.
findings.limitations: Counting themes in a best-customer sample shows what is common among them, not market size.

findings.summary: Solve for one Job at a time. Choose using urgency, willingness to pay, low support or sales burden, retention potential, expansion potential, whether those customers gather where they can be reached, and wildcards such as vision, unfair advantage and fit with a self-serve or sales-led motion.
findings.limitations: Unweighted checklist; no scale or tie-break.

findings.summary: Alistair ($2M ARR, 5,000 customers, flat growth) filtered to 500 healthiest customers, found two Jobs (beginners vs experienced marketers wanting automation), refocused site copy on the experienced group, and reports +89% trial signups and +40% trial-to-paid.
findings.limitations: Self-reported; criteria table column marks unreadable in extraction.

findings.summary: Generic models (buyer journey, AARRR pirate metrics) force all businesses into the same few stages and reward business-value moments like signup or paid, rather than the customer getting value.
findings.limitations: Critique of stage naming and incentives; the book still uses sequential stages.

findings.summary: Map the chosen Job's experience into three phases (Struggle, Evaluation, Growth), each described by what the customer thinks, does and feels; split phases into milestones where feelings shift. Typical milestones: Problem and Interest; First Value and Value Realization; Continued Value and Value Growth. Evaluation milestones vary most (enterprise vs small business).
findings.limitations: Built per Job from best-customer data; workshop method, not validated.

findings.summary: An Airbnb wall journey seen by Gia inspired Unbounce's first customer-experience map; reported revenue +864% two years after it was used company-wide.
findings.limitations: Correlation over a high-growth period.

findings.summary: Metrics shape behaviour: two teams sharing one lead metric led to misattribution; ticket-closure speed rewards boilerplate replies. Tie team performance to customer success.
findings.limitations: Anecdotal.

findings.summary: Active-user logins are not value for products that work in the background; measure the action that shows the customer got the value they wanted (FeedOtter example: newsletters sent consistently without errors).

Lagging indicators (ARR/MRR, CAC, ARPU, LTV) report results; leading indicators (new unique visits, signups, activation, engagement, expansion, referrals/reviews, NPS, CSAT) are actions teams can act on. Assign leading indicators to milestones.
findings.limitations: Lists signups and NPS/CSAT as leading despite warning elsewhere against transactional and opinion measures.

findings.summary: Each milestone gets a KPI that is trackable, marks a leap of faith into the next milestone, and shows the team did its job. Use new unique visits, not total traffic, for Problem. For Evaluation, map what customers said was valuable to the features that create it, and set First Value and Value Realization as feature-usage thresholds. Continued Value repeats the value KPI per period; Value Growth adds upgrade, review or referral. SparkToro thresholds are the worked example.
findings.limitations: Thresholds set by judgment from research; no step to validate them against later payment or retention.

findings.summary: Build dashboards for milestone KPIs and benchmark current performance before choosing work.
findings.limitations: Requires event tracking.

findings.summary: A success gap is a mismatch between what ideal customers need and what the experience provides. Find gaps by walking each milestone as the customer would; pick one gap, typically where many reach a milestone but few reach the next and a modest lift has outsized revenue effect, also weighing payoff, use of existing resources, short-term actionability and a clear path.
findings.limitations: Walk-through is a heuristic audit; causes are hypotheses.

findings.summary: Shortlist a few projects deliverable in weeks or months that bridge only the chosen gap; park ideas for other gaps; measure with the milestone KPI; schedule recurring health checks. The book offers a per-milestone menu of typical project types (e.g. onboarding changes at First Value, win-back and 'why wasn't it right' emails at Value Realization, upgrade and review asks at Value Growth).
findings.limitations: Menu is illustrative.

findings.summary: Reported cases: SparkToro's in-app checklist plus onboarding emails doubled free-to-paid conversion in two months; CareerCake cut lead-to-call time from one month to three days (book calls it a 90% increase in velocity, which is actually a 90% reduction in time); Life Lapse visitor-to-user 9.42% to 18.19% (+93%) and sales +18.9% in 50 days; HiringBranch four qualified inbound leads within 12 days of a new site.
findings.limitations: Single-company before/after reports, short windows, no controls; one mislabelled percentage.

findings.summary: Keep the map in use: every plan and project brief names the Job, milestone and KPI it supports; set targets on the new KPIs; tie research from different teams to map stages; use the map in employee onboarding.
Iterate by returning to a tabled Job or by rerunning the process for a segment or market not yet served well.
findings.limitations: No refresh cadence given.

findings.summary: The relationship is better pictured as a circle than a line for recurring revenue, because value can keep expanding.
findings.limitations: Metaphor.

findings.summary: Foreword: a home builder added the most-requested feature from a focus group, but buyers chose a cheaper competing upgrade at the price point; watching sales and asking recent buyers revealed the gap between what people say and what they do.
findings.limitations: Anecdote.

findings.summary: Early sales happens in two stages: first work out whether the product solves a paid-for pain, then scale the selling. Using scale-stage methods before product-market fit does real damage.
findings.limitations: Written for venture-backed B2B SaaS; 'fit' is not defined in measurable terms.

findings.summary: At the start the founder has to do the selling. Professional reps sell a proven offer to a known persona and can't tell a sales failure from a product failure. The author calls early selling 'evangelical': part product management, part product marketing.
findings.limitations: Based on the author's experience at TalentBin and others; not tested.

findings.summary: Early on, work that doesn't scale is fine and worth doing, such as on-site visits for a product under $1,000 a year or building lead lists by hand. Treat it as paying for information.
findings.limitations: For an owner-operator, those hours have a real cost. ClimbOS already prices owner time in cacFull (shared/growth/calc.ts:35).

findings.summary: Two anti-patterns: buying poorly targeted lists instead of building your own, and believing you can sell with no sales reps at all.
findings.limitations: The objection to lists is about targeting quality, not legality.

findings.summary: Time is the scarce thing in selling. Drop marginal opportunities quickly. Poor-fit customers who buy anyway soak up support time, churn and speak badly of the product.
findings.limitations: Asserted, not measured.

findings.summary: Put activity first: template every message, proofread once and move on, and stop over-preparing for each touch.
findings.limitations: Read as a call for volume, this clashes with ClimbOS's evidence-per-prospect rule and today's deliverability limits.

findings.summary: Record everything, including honest loss reasons, so you or a colleague can pick an account up again months later.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: For a new, innovative solution, a 20-30% win rate (counted from the point sales gets a prospect) is called solid.
findings.limitations: Anecdotal, SaaS of about 2011-2015, and the denominator isn't defined. Don't use it as a ClimbOS base rate.

findings.summary: Selling runs on numbers: emails per demo, opportunities per deal, and average contract value to judge whether you can afford a setter.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: Build the narrative as problem, then solution, then specifics: the problem, who has it, what it costs, how it's solved today and why that falls short, what has changed, how the new solution works, proof, and price. Because the order builds step by step, you can stop as soon as the prospect rejects the problem.
findings.limitations: Tuned for new-technology B2B; 'what has changed' may not exist for many small service businesses.

findings.summary: The person with the problem is whoever is functionally responsible for fixing it: the budget holder, or the person who spends the hours on it. The owner role changes with company size (CEO, then a director, then a specialist). If an account has no one in that role, it is probably not qualified.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: Cost of the problem comes in three kinds: hard ROI (a direct cost avoided), soft ROI (opportunity cost that needs other actions to realise), and directional benefits that are hard to quantify. Work out unit costs, then scale them to the prospect's size. Example: going from 8 to 10 deals of $8,000 a month is 25% more, or $16,000 per rep per month.
findings.limitations: The worked figures are the author's illustration, not data.

findings.summary: Today's answer to the problem is one of four: no solution, a manual process, a service provider, or a product. If a prospect already pays a provider or for a product, that is a good qualification sign. Admit what the alternatives do well, or the story won't be credible.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: Name the change that makes a new solution possible, or necessary, and keep checking whether the trend still supports the narrative.
findings.limitations: Encourages a trend claim even where none is real; positioning skill step 8 is stricter.

findings.summary: Prove superiority in the metrics the buyer already tracks. Qualitative claims are extras and ideally have numbers behind them. Customer counts, testimonials and press are supporting evidence.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: Charge from the first sale. Start lowish and raise prices as reactions come in. TalentBin went from $99 a month to $499 a month, then settled at $6,000 per seat per year against about $8,000 for LinkedIn Recruiter. Grandfather early customers.
findings.limitations: One company's pricing in about 2012-2014. The 'buy now before it goes up' line is false urgency unless a rise is really planned.

findings.summary: Early pricing methods: copy the price structure of comparable products (one innovation at a time), set ROI-based prices from a defensible value model, tie price to a value metric, price under budget thresholds (personal card, team card, department discretionary budget), don't price so high that everything must go right, and don't add tiers before segments are known.
findings.limitations: The HIRABL example (1 recoverable fee per 500 submissions, $15,000 average fee, about 10x ROI on $20,000) is the vendor's own claim.

findings.summary: Favour speed over polish. A minimum deck is one slide per narrative step. Keep a master deck you never send. Add an appendix slide the second time a question comes up. Keep a short leave-behind deck separate from the presenting deck.
findings.limitations: Tools named (ClearSlide, DocSend, Camtasia, Jing) are dated.

findings.summary: Tailor materials with evidence about the prospect, such as their own search results, careers page or website, in the deck and the demo. A personalised screenshot takes about a minute; a short recorded walk-through takes about five.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: The author suggests showing customer logos in live presentations without asking, putting publicity rights into an agreement most customers won't read, writing testimonials for customers to approve, and thanking them with merchandise or gift cards.
findings.limitations: Conflicts with ClimbOS: cold-outreach allows named customers only with permission, and lint.ts blocks unsourced claims. Paying for testimonials can require a disclosure under the FTC endorsement guides.

findings.summary: Cold-email templates: assume the pain because you prospected for it, put a qualifier in the subject, keep it plain text and about the prospect, include 'click targets' (video links) so you can track interest, end with a direct ask for a 20-minute meeting, and split the message into one value theme per email for a drip sequence.
findings.limitations: The sample templates run 100-200+ words with exclamation marks and claims (for example 'thousands of customers'). Links and tracking conflict with the cold-outreach skill.

findings.summary: Warm intros: first qualify the account, then find a shared connection. Send that person a short reason plus a ready-to-forward email, so the target opts in. Don't ask for a direct cold introduction. If the forward gets no answer, follow up with the target once in the same thread.
findings.limitations: Using a tracking pixel to see whether the intro was forwarded conflicts with the no-tracking rule.

findings.summary: Phone scripts should take 30-90 seconds, with ready responses for the likely replies. Treat voicemail as audio email and always pair it with an email.
findings.limitations: No mention of call-compliance rules (TPS/CTPS, TCPA).

findings.summary: Order the demo by importance, because it may end early. Build it around the buyer's workflow and their own context, researched in advance rather than asked on the call. The strongest version runs on the prospect's own data (HIRABL found missed fees before the call).
findings.limitations: Detailed demo craft is in Chapter 7 (other agent).

findings.summary: A rough 1-5 minute overview video recorded on a laptop beats a polished explainer that isn't finished. Host on YouTube for trust and search.
findings.limitations: The platform advice is from 2015.

findings.summary: First goal: 50-100 accounts that have the pain. Don't pick prospects because they're easy to reach (friends, incubator peers). Twenty demos to poor-fit prospects at about two hours each (30 minutes prep, 60 demo, 30 follow-up) burn about a week.
findings.limitations: The time figures are illustrative.

findings.summary: Write the ICP as account-level characteristics that signal demand: minimum requirements plus how much demand there is. Some can be seen publicly, others can only be learned by asking (discovery calls, forms). Weigh them into an attractiveness score. The ICP describes an organisation, not a person.
findings.limitations: No weights given; the score is qualitative.

findings.summary: Sources for building the list: people searches, directories and maps for local businesses, competitors' or marketplaces' public listings, licence databases, website technology detection, hiring pages, and visible paid-tier badges as a sign of willingness to pay. Combine sources to enrich an account, but source accounts from one productive place; flitting between sources is a discipline problem. Avoid list vendors as stale and thin.
findings.limitations: The named tools (Data.com, Datanyze, Rapportive, WANTED) are 2015-era, and some are gone. The LinkedIn premium search methods conflict with the ClimbOS no-LinkedIn-scraping rule if automated.

findings.summary: Rabbits, deer, elephants: start with mid-sized accounts that are big enough to feel the pain, small enough to decide fast, and not locked into legacy systems, leaning toward the larger ones. Start in your own area so in-person meetings are possible.
findings.limitations: Size bands are relative to the product; no thresholds given.

findings.summary: Choose account-first or contact-first by whichever required trait rules accounts out most cheaply: people with a role for TalentBin, a required software stack for Immediately.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: The point of contact owns the pain and holds the budget, and their title varies by company stage. Collect several related contacts per account. 'Complementary' decision makers (the internal customer of the problem owner) are a fallback. Going to the CEO first is risky because of email volume and assistants. Bottom-up selling via users comes later. Look for shared connections only after the account qualifies.
findings.limitations: Grabbing every contact at once can lead to several simultaneous cold emails into one account.

findings.summary: Finding addresses: search for published addresses, use profile pages, and use personal addresses (the author calls worries about this overblown). Build the address from the company's naming pattern and check it with plugins, or use LinkedIn email-finder tools. For local businesses, phone comes first.
findings.limitations: Conflicts directly with ClimbOS policy: published-verbatim only (shared/outbound/index.ts:188-209); no personal addresses or LinkedIn scraping (skills/prospecting step 6); pattern guessing blocked in CA/AU and capped at 3 elsewhere.

findings.summary: Appointment setting sells the meeting, not the product. A founder can frame it as research, but the conversation has to stay commercial.
findings.limitations: None notable.

findings.summary: Outreach (vendor) data the author cites: a hand-customised first email got up to 12% response against 5% for no personalisation. Step 2 had the highest response (18%), steps 3-5 held around 13-17%, a seven-step drip got about 15x the responses of a single email, and a 'break-up' last email nudges replies.
findings.limitations: Vendor-run, undated (about 2015), unknown denominators; the graphs are images. Contradicts the cold-outreach skill's vendor figure that 58% of replies come from the first email.

findings.summary: Track opens and clicks in every email, and call or email again right after an open.
findings.limitations: Opens have been unreliable since Apple Mail Privacy Protection (2021). Tracking hurts deliverability and is banned in ClimbOS cold steps (cold-outreach step 7; spam-and-ai-tells.md:5).

findings.summary: Send times: avoid Monday mornings; try mid-morning Tuesday, early morning (6-7am) or evening (7-8pm).
findings.limitations: No data. Conflicts with the sales-follow-up skill's sensible-hours rule and the 8:00-17:00 weekday window in shared/outbound/sending.ts:39-42.

findings.summary: Time calls to the prospect's working day: for example, a restaurant between lunch and dinner service. With gatekeepers: don't lie, be pleasant, give a one-line value statement, ask for the direct line. The author describes, but doesn't recommend, misleading voicemails such as pretending to return a call.
findings.limitations: The 'hero or in the doghouse' gatekeeper framing leans on mild fear.

findings.summary: Book the slot during the call, not over email. Keep it within a week, ideally two or three days out. Collect contact details and offer to invite other relevant people. If they want to talk right away, give a short 'demo-lite' and book the full demo.
findings.limitations: The claim that attendance falls after a week is unquantified.

findings.summary: On objections to booking ('call me later', 'no budget', 'send info', 'we use X', feature questions, price, 'not my decision'), keep pressing for the meeting. Tactics include asking for 30 seconds now, a guilt angle, holding back the price, and hinting you'll go to their boss.
findings.limitations: Conflicts with ClimbOS reply-handling (permission-based check-ins, no arguing) and sales-follow-up (answer price from facts; accept a second no).

findings.summary: Meeting hygiene: always send a calendar invite with the location in both the location field and the description, a short agenda, a clear title and everyone who should attend. Block 15-30 minutes before and after. Send an email reminder the morning of the meeting rather than early calendar alerts. TalentBin treated each demo as worth $5,000, from average contract value times win rate.
findings.limitations: The $5,000 is one company's figure.

findings.summary: Cadence: alternate email, call and voicemail over about a week (example: days 1, 2, 3, 5 and a break-up on day 7), and reprioritise by engagement.
findings.limitations: Much more intense than ClimbOS's email-only 0/3/7/14 day sequence; relies on open signals.

findings.summary: Inbound basics: outbound creates inbound. Offer one clear demo request. Ask only for name, company, title, email and phone, plus the qualifiers you can't find yourself; show a phone number; send an automatic reply. Respond within minutes. The cited MIT/InsideSales study found contact rates about 100x lower at 30 minutes than at 5. Make about six attempts before moving on. Qualify the account, not just the lead. Use a 'hard qualifier' email for likely misfits.
findings.limitations: The lead-response study is roughly 2007-2011 and vendor co-authored. The claim that each attempt adds 15% (about 90% by six) is a simplification.

findings.summary: Inconsistency within the book: the HIRABL missed-fee rate is 1 per 500 submissions in Ch 2 but 1 in 300 permanent submissions in the Ch 6 template.
findings.limitations: Shows that vendor figures in templates can't be reused as facts.

findings.summary: The TalentBin templates sell candidates' personal email addresses gathered by crawling the web. The book's own model relies on scraped personal data.
findings.limitations: Under GDPR and current platform terms this would need a lawful basis; flagged as a policy conflict.

findings.summary: Pitching is persuading the buyer and other stakeholders that the pain exists, is big enough to fix, that this offer fixes it, that the value will be captured, and that it must be done now rather than later; it also means admitting early when a deal will not close.

Persuasion model: likelihood and size of a sale depend on potential value x how well the buyer understands that value x how much they believe they will capture it. Buyers discount for disbelief. Raise value by targeting high-pain accounts, comprehension by clear presentation, belief by proof, tailored demos and pilots.
findings.limitations: Conceptual multiplicative model; not measured or calibrated.

findings.summary: Revenue = opportunities worked x win rate x average deal size. Early on the author prefers in-person selling for trust and learning, accepting fewer meetings; at scale, remote selling for volume.
findings.limitations: Pre-2020-remote norms; the in-person preference is a 2020 view for tech B2B.

findings.summary: Block about 15 minutes of pre-call planning before every demo. Hypothetical: with a $20,000 deal, lifting win rate from 15% to 25% is worth $2,000 of expected revenue per demo. Do not research before cold calls (low connect rates make it wasteful).
findings.limitations: Hypothetical figures.

findings.summary: Author expectations: demo hold (show-up) rates should be 80% or higher; each scheduled meeting carries roughly a 10-20% chance of being missed and rescheduled.
findings.limitations: Author practitioner estimate for US tech B2B, ~2010s; no dataset. Grade D.

findings.summary: Pre-call checklist: visible pain signals and 'size of prize' (how much the account could buy), current and competing tools, capacity to pay, likely users, stakeholders and influencers, data to customise the demo, rapport topics, the 'known unknowns' to ask in discovery, and a stated goal for the call. Save it in the CRM.

Pitch order: brief rapport, discovery, a few slides to set the mental model, a live tailored demo, proof (ROI, customer evidence), then pricing and a direct ask. Split off a short separate discovery call only when the demo is long; early on keep them together, since every extra meeting adds a no-show risk.
Different people need different value language: end users (easier job, career), first-line managers (team efficiency, ROI, budget), executives (company revenue, cash, valuation).

Discovery (first 5-10 minutes, framed as for the buyer's benefit) both qualifies and arms the pitch. BANT, ANUM and ChAMP are named. For new-category offers, strict budget/timeline tests misfire because buyers did not know the solution existed; weight pain size, urgency, whether they buy tools for problems at all, who decides, and ability to pay. Use researched facts to ask specific, verifiable questions. Keep a living question list.

Cascade pain questions: the size of the problem, how it is solved today, the downsides of that, and the consequences of not solving it. Tie questions to features. Then ask about users, decision authority, buying cycle and discretionary budget directly.

During the presentation, repeat key points, check attention and understanding with specific questions (giving permission not to know), keep discovering as topics arise ('rolling discovery'), build agreement point by point, slow down, and drop slides or features that do not fit this buyer.

Micro-contracts (attributed to Sandler 'upfront contracts'): before each step, say what you propose and why and get agreement; restate the agreement at the start of the next meeting. A prospect breaking agreed steps is an early warning; name it directly and ask whether it is still a priority.

If discovery shows no pain or no ability to pay, end the call politely and give the time back; if only the contact lacks authority, partner with them to reach the decision-maker. Good prequalification should make this rare.

The demo should prove the promises with the buyer's own data where possible, or demo-ready data that shows the use cases cleanly; prioritise features tied to discovery; follow the demo with proof (ROI, customer results) before pricing.

Founders most often fail by not presenting price and not asking for the sale. Let the buyer ask for price or use a trial close ('is this useful for X?'); present unit price framed against current spend, alternatives or ROI, then stay silent; ask directly. Send proposals only to buyers who said they want to buy; options can steer to a larger purchase (three options, middle as target).
findings.limitations: Option-steering advice conflicts with Book 11 §6 (see disagreements).

findings.summary: Objections signal engagement. Ask what specifically blocks progress. Generic types: no authority, no need, happy with status quo / fear of change, timing, price/value, no budget, needs a trial or reference; plus solution-specific and competitor objections. Handle as a loop: catch it, find the question under the question, answer with numeric and qualitative proof, check understanding, return to the close; repeat until none remain.

Price objections: first ask how far apart you are. A small gap (author's example ~10%) is a discount negotiation; a large gap (~50%) is a value disagreement, so walk the value math and invite the buyer to find the flaw. A valid reason (lower value for this buyer, partial use, a cheaper existing workaround) can justify a documented concession or a new package; record the rationale so it is not treated as the standard price. Do not sell to buyers who will get little value.

'No budget': if the organisation never buys tools for problems, that is a disqualifier, not an objection. Otherwise look for budget already spent on the problem, renewals that can be reallocated, discretionary or one-off budget, a later start date, or monthly payment at a higher total.

Trial requests usually mean 'I need more proof'. Ask what proof they need (often case studies or references). Offer a group demo or a guided hands-on session. Run a structured pilot (success criteria, training, check-ins, instrumented use) only for large deals. Avoid unstructured trials unless the product is built for self-serve value.

Recurring objections get an appendix slide and an entry in a living objection document; very frequent ones are addressed proactively in the pitch. Competitor questions are reframed to the full evaluation criteria rather than one feature.

After every meeting: state the concrete next action and who does what, calendar any follow-up meeting, put the agreement in writing, deliver your part quickly (buyer commitment decays with time), and send a summary email with the deck.

Negotiation levers are unit price, quantity, contract length, payment terms and auto-renewal. Priority for an early company is cash up front, then term length. Give ground one step at a time and trade (lower unit price for more units or longer term; lower total for less scope; shorter terms and split payments priced higher). To match a competitor's quote, see it and require signature the same day to avoid a reverse auction.
findings.limitations: Author's short-term pricing rule (per-month price 2-3x the annual rate) is not met by his own example: $5,000 for 6 months vs $7,000 for 12 is 1.43x per month.

findings.summary: Author ranges: new-solution win rates of 10-20% are typical and 30% is very good; winning every deal suggests too few or cherry-picked opportunities.
findings.limitations: Author's practitioner view, US tech B2B, ~2010s. Grade D.

findings.summary: Close a deal as lost after a direct no, a run of broken micro-contracts, or going dark; a short, respectful email asking for clarity often resolves it. Record the reason (competitor picklist plus notes). Re-engage at the time the buyer named or, if none, after about 60 days, as a new opportunity.
findings.limitations: The 60-day default re-contact conflicts with ClimbOS consent rules (see disagreements).

findings.summary: TalentBin's stages: Demo Scheduled, Qualified, Seeking Approval, Sent Proposal, Negotiation, Verbal Agreement, Contract Sent, Closed Won, Closed Lost, Closed-Unqualified (a demo that should never have happened, reviewed to fix targeting). He dismisses CRM default stage probabilities as unhelpful at early stage and admits 'Qualified' became a catch-all.

Every open deal needs an explicit, calendared next step. Hold a weekly pipeline review. Your 'carrying load' is exceeded when close rates fall; then cap new demos. Work closest to the money first, ranked by value x ease. Flag deals with no activity for 7 days in late stages, stuck over about 2 weeks in a stage, or with no future meeting ('uncovered'). Clean ruthlessly.

Time-block selling roles (prospecting, outreach, follow-up, demos, pipeline). Mondays and Fridays show more cancellations (anecdotal). Once the founder can reliably set appointments, add an appointment setter so the founder spends time on demos and closing; worked example of SDR plus AE cost of sales.
findings.limitations: Salary figures are 2010s US.

findings.summary: Customer success means delivering what the sale promised (the KPIs in the sales narrative). The attention window right after purchase is the cheapest time to drive adoption. A chart (image; values in text) shows a hypothetical business at ~$4M MRR after 58 months with no churn, ~$2.8M at 2.5% monthly churn, under $2M at 5%, over $7M with 2.5% monthly net expansion.
findings.limitations: Hypothetical chart; inputs not given, so not reproducible.

findings.summary: Implementation must complete every precondition for success. Check that its labour cost fits the price: 120 minutes per customer by a $50k-a-year rep doing 15 a week is about $70 each, which a $20-a-month product cannot carry. Heavy implementations can carry a one-off fee of about 3x the labour cost.
findings.limitations: $70 implies ~48 working weeks (50,000/(48x15)=69.4); 52 weeks gives 64.1.

findings.summary: Implementation calls: prepare like a sales call; open with 'rediscovery' (restate the buyer's goal and confirm it); do setup blockers first; have the user do real work; prefer one-to-one over group sessions early; set measurable homework and book a back-check about two weeks out before ending; give a support contact and recording; chase missed sessions; re-implement when users or sponsors change.

Multi-step implementations: kickoff with sponsors, a shared tracker (item, owner, date, status), status emails, polite escalation, and a formal 'now operational' notice so sponsors start expecting results.

Support: make contact easy, acknowledge fast, empathise and take the blame, track ticket state until the customer confirms it is solved, build canned answers and help articles for repeated questions, and tag tickets for product decisions.

Monitor value precursors and outcomes (logins, key actions, results). Act on struggling users with a helping frame; spend most effort on middling ('C+/B-') users rather than the best or worst. Capture outcomes in product or check-ins/NPS as time-stamped records. Run quarterly success reviews (goals restated, KPIs before vs after, issues and fixes, next steps; upsell only when delivering); for low-price products, send an automated review. Announce releases to users and decision-makers.

Renewals: an auto-renew clause plus a courtesy notice; for manual renewals a review-style call about 6 weeks before term end (final QBR about 3 months out); if blockers appear, a short free extension; always ask for the renewal; use next-year goals to find upsell.
findings.limitations: Auto-renewal terms are regulated in many jurisdictions; not discussed by the author.

findings.summary: Customer success feeds product (ticket tags), sales (references, champions who change jobs) and marketing (proof). Early on one person can own implementation, support, reviews and renewal; specialise later.

Scaling means adding proven units of sellers. Two failure modes: premature scaling (hiring sales to 'figure it out' before the motion works, burning cash and acquiring bad-fit customers) and lagged scaling (founder keeps closing instead of packaging the motion). Readiness: a reliable win rate in the author's 'good' band with consistent deal size and cycle; if win rate is low, fix messaging, product or pricing before adding volume.
Author ranges: a good B2B win rate is 15-30% of first meetings; total sales cost should stay around 20-30% of the revenue it closes (e.g. a $100k rep should book about $500k).
findings.limitations: Venture-backed SaaS context; not a small-business or agency benchmark. Grade D.

findings.summary: Author's accounts of premature scaling: Zenefits (selling customers it could not serve profitably, then layoffs) and Square Stand in 2014 (hiring ~20 senior AEs before product fit in a higher-end segment).
findings.limitations: Author's secondhand narrative; not independently verified here.

findings.summary: Maturity stages with exit criteria: founder does everything (a handful of paying, successful, renewing customers) -> founder plus appointment setter or CS help (a few dozen successful customers and a documented motion) -> founder plus two sellers (they sell at least as efficiently) -> a full pod that pays for itself -> cloned pods.

Metrics harness: set the goal, document the expected activity mix, record activity, review it on a fixed cadence, detect anomalies against goals and peers, trace root causes down a metric tree (bookings -> deals x deal size -> opportunities x win rate -> activity), inspect calls, then coach. Track quantity metrics first, quality ratios (win rate, deal size, cycle, time in stage, untouched deals) next.

Operational cadence: standups, weekly team meeting, weekly pipeline review, biweekly one-on-ones, monthly retrospective; each meeting with purpose, anti-purpose, attendees, format, length. A manager loses track beyond roughly 6-9 reports (conventional wisdom).

Hiring (skimmed): add roles in order of the binding sales constraint: appointment setting first, more closers when the closer's calendar is full, account management when renewals pile up. Match candidates to your sales-cycle tempo. Screen closers with a mock presentation checking discovery, agreement-building, objection handling and asking for the sale.
Compensation (skimmed): new-business AEs about 50/50 base/variable, appointment setters and account managers 60/40-70/30; San Francisco 2010s salary bands are given.
findings.limitations: Region- and era-specific; not for use in ClimbOS outputs.

findings.summary: Onboarding (skimmed): train hires in cohorts; drill the demo section by section, then paired sparring; give new closers high-intent inbound ('bluebird') deals first; review calls rather than sitting in; watch ramp KPIs (hold rate, win/loss, activity, stuck deals). Cites a traditional 30-50% early flameout rate he believes better onboarding reduces.
findings.limitations: Flameout rate is an unsourced industry claim.

findings.summary: Hire a sales leader only after several sellers sell at least as well as the founder; look for a hands-on manager from a similar-stage company with a similar sales motion.

findings.summary: Double jeopardy: within a category, smaller brands have far fewer buyers and those buyers buy slightly less often; average purchase frequency varies little across brands while penetration varies a lot.
findings.limitations: Mostly consumer-panel data for repeat-purchase categories; cross-sectional regularity across competing brands, not a causal law for one firm; says nothing about supply limits.

findings.summary: Growth targets should be built on penetration; plans that need large loyalty or frequency gains swim against the law (e.g. a small shampoo brand would need more purchases than its buyers make in the whole category).
findings.limitations: Applies where the brand is one of many substitutes in a stable category.

findings.summary: Effectiveness-awards analyses (IPA): most cases reporting growth reported penetration growth (82%) vs loyalty-only (2%); campaigns targeting penetration won more often; Kraft internal study found penetration drove share for 67 brands.
findings.limitations: Award entries are self-selected success stories; large advertisers; 1990s-2013 data.

findings.summary: Double jeopardy also shown in an industrial market (ready-mix concrete suppliers to builders, West Yorkshire) and claimed for services, stores, media and politicians.
findings.limitations: One small B2B dataset; supplier counts and buyer counts are small; no SaaS or contract-service evidence.

findings.summary: A true niche brand has unusually high loyalty for its share; Sharp treats most 'niche' brands as brands with a penetration deficit caused by missing physical or mental availability (or a differentiation that some buyers reject).
findings.limitations: Viewed from a brand-share perspective; does not consider a deliberate beachhead strategy where narrow scope is chosen for learning or capacity.

findings.summary: Cross-selling metrics (products per customer) barely differ between competing insurers or banks and follow double jeopardy; dramatic cross-sell gains are rare and the metric is easy to inflate.
findings.limitations: Two Australian financial-services datasets.

findings.summary: Heavy-buyer fallacy: current heavy customers are not the best growth investment because they already buy most of what they will; tenure did not predict lifetime profit in cited retail and brokerage studies.
findings.limitations: Cited studies are consumer/catalogue/brokerage; account-based B2B with expansion revenue not tested.

findings.summary: The 'retaining 5% more customers boosts profit ~100%' claim is a thought experiment that assumed a costless halving of defection; the 'acquisition costs five times retention' maxim has no cited empirical support.
findings.limitations: Critique of a 1990 article; does not prove retention work is never worthwhile.

findings.summary: Defection rates follow double jeopardy: smaller brands lose a larger share of their customers each year; in a stable two-brand market the small brand's defection rate is mechanically higher (100 of 200 = 50% vs 100 of 800 = 12.5%).
findings.limitations: Car and bank data; assumes stable shares; subscription churn caused by poor product value is not the case studied.

findings.summary: Growth potential from eliminating defection is small compared with acquisition: a car brand with ~50% defection could gain about one share point from zero defection versus tens of points up for grabs through acquisition; service categories with 3-5% annual defection gain only a few points.
findings.limitations: Depends on low or category-normal defection; does not hold when a firm's churn is far above its category norm.

findings.summary: Brands that grew did so mainly through unusually high acquisition, while defection stayed at the norm for their size; declining brands had poor acquisition (pharma, chocolate, banking panel studies).
findings.limitations: Mature categories; no early-stage or subscription-software cases.

findings.summary: Much defection is outside marketer control (moving house, no longer needing the service, head-office directives); a small regional bank's higher defection is explained by its branch footprint, not satisfaction.
findings.limitations: Bank data; voluntary value-driven churn in software is a different mix.

findings.summary: Most buyers of any brand are light buyers; even for Coca-Cola about half of buyers bought it once or twice a year; ultra-heavy buyers are few and comparatively unresponsive to advertising.
findings.limitations: Frequently bought consumer goods; Figs 4.1-4.3 are images (values from text).

findings.summary: Pareto is not 80/20: the heaviest 20% of a brand's buyers typically deliver about half of volume over a year (about 35% over a quarter); Goodhardt's 20:30:50 rule; the ratio depends on the analysis period.
findings.limitations: FMCG panels; B2B revenue concentration by account (contract size) is a different quantity.

findings.summary: Law of buyer moderation: in the next period heavy buyers buy less, light buyers more, and some non-buyers buy, with no real change in behaviour (regression to the mean); e.g. a stable sauce brand got 14% of next-year volume from prior non-buyers.
findings.limitations: Data from US household panels; strongest over short periods.

findings.summary: When a brand grows, buying propensities rise across all buyer weights, so marketing has the best chance when it reaches as many category buyers as possible, especially light and non-buyers; acquisition is vital even to stand still.
findings.limitations: Assumes the cost to reach light buyers is affordable (mass media era); small budgets face a minimum-reach problem.

findings.summary: Competing brands sell to near-identical customer profiles (demographics, values, media); deliberate extreme targeting still produced normal customer bases once share was won.
findings.limitations: Differences remain for price tier, function and geography (which Sharp calls obvious).

findings.summary: Duplication of purchase law: a brand shares customers with each rival in line with the rival's size; partitions exist but are usually slight and driven by function or availability rather than image; use it to define the category broadly and to predict cannibalisation.
findings.limitations: Needs buyer-level purchase data across brands; a small business rarely has it.

findings.summary: Loyalty is natural but divided (repertoires); 100% loyal buyers are a minority and mostly light category buyers; larger brands have proportionally more light category buyers (natural monopoly law).
findings.limitations: Opportunity matters: fewer purchases or fewer options on offer raise apparent loyalty.

findings.summary: Brand attitudes and image beliefs are probabilistic: about half of people who agree with a brand statement repeat it in a second interview; usage drives attitudes more than the reverse.
findings.limitations: Survey-based; applies to image items rather than hard functional facts.

findings.summary: Brand fanatics are few and worth little in revenue (Harley segmentation: the most attitudinally loyal segments were a small share of revenue); new customers give more word of mouth than long-term ones; Apple's repeat-purchase loyalty was only slightly above the double-jeopardy expectation, explained by switching costs.
findings.limitations: Single-brand cases; Harley data from 1995; Apple surveys n=400-901 in 2011.

findings.summary: Perceived differentiation is low and similar across rivals: on average about 10% of a brand's users call it different or unique (Millward Brown's independent data: 18% among those who find the brand acceptable); higher scores attach to small premium brands or obvious functional differences.
findings.limitations: Survey wording effects; consumer and retail-bank categories; says little about new B2B products where buyers do compare features.

findings.summary: Distinctiveness, not differentiation: build and protect distinctive brand assets (colours, logos, characters, taglines, styles) judged on fame (share of people who link the asset to the brand) and uniqueness (share who link it only to that brand); consistency over years is required.
findings.limitations: Asset research is costly; small firms rarely have survey budgets.

findings.summary: Brand advertising's sales effect is real but thin and spread over time; single-source data shows it; reach matters more than frequency and continuous presence beats bursts with gaps.
findings.limitations: Mostly TV and FMCG single-source studies.

findings.summary: In one Australian TV study only about 40% of ads were recognised and about 40% of those correctly branded, so roughly 16% of exposures passed both hurdles.
findings.limitations: One unpublished study of 143 TV ads.

findings.summary: Exception: in categories where people only pay attention shortly before buying (mortgages, insurance, furniture, travel, emergency trades) advertising has more immediate effect; directory and search ads can persuade with plain information.
findings.limitations: Stated briefly; not quantified.

findings.summary: Price promotions lift sales only while they run; nearly all promo buyers had bought the brand before; no lasting purchase-reinforcement effect for established brands; frequent promotions raise price sensitivity and invite retaliation.
findings.limitations: Grocery/FMCG; new-product trial promotions not covered.

findings.summary: Average temporary-promotion price elasticity about -2.3 to -2.6 (one study -4.0), usually between -1 and -4; elasticity is bigger when the price crosses a big rival, the cut is signalled, the brand is small, the change is an increase, or the brand's price is near the category average.
findings.limitations: Meta-analyses of consumer goods; ranges are wide.

findings.summary: Short-term promo profit depends on margin, cut depth and elasticity; the needed sales lift is cut/(margin - cut) (e.g. 30% margin, 10% cut needs +50%); keep cuts shallow; count the post-promo dip and competitor matching.
findings.limitations: Table 10.2 has one inconsistent cell (40% margin, 5% cut shows 10%, arithmetic gives 14.3%).

findings.summary: In-store promotions have very low reach (e.g. 10% retailer share x 20% fortnightly category penetration = 2% of buyers); advertising reaches many with a small nudge; prefer feature/advertising support over deep cuts.
findings.limitations: Retail-distributed brands.

findings.summary: Loyalty programs produce small, inconsistent loyalty effects and little growth because they recruit existing buyers; member vs non-member comparisons are biased by selection and buyer moderation.
findings.limitations: Large coalition/supermarket programs; small venue programs not studied.

findings.summary: Mental availability = the propensity for a brand to be noticed or thought of in buying situations, built from many fresh memory links to category cues; competitors are 'cue competitors', not just look-alikes.
findings.limitations: Measurement needs cue-based surveys.

findings.summary: Physical availability shows a convex (reverse-L) link to share: very broad distribution (about 80%+ weighted) is necessary but not sufficient for high share.
findings.limitations: Retail-distributed packaged goods.

findings.summary: Seven rules: reach all category buyers continuously; be easy to buy; get noticed; refresh and build brand-linked memories; create distinctive assets; be consistent yet fresh; stay competitive and remove reasons not to buy (including an excessive price later patched with discounts).
findings.limitations: Rules of thumb drawn from the laws; no direct tests for small firms.

findings.summary: FAQ: the laws are claimed to apply to small, service and B2B brands; new brands should plant basic memories (what it is, looks like, where sold) and may grow one geography at a time to win share of voice there; spend any budget evenly (about one twelfth a month).
findings.limitations: Assertions, not new evidence.

findings.summary: Growing a category by teaching new uses rarely works for one brand's budget; habits are sticky; it works better when backed by physical availability changes.
findings.limitations: Few cases; arguable for genuinely new categories.
