findings.summary: Double jeopardy: smaller brands have many fewer buyers who are also slightly less loyal. The authors report it for packaged goods, services (banks, insurance), durables, retailers, social sites, two B2B examples (concrete suppliers, coronary stents) and many emerging markets.
findings.limitations: Evidence is mostly panel and survey data on repeat categories. B2B support is two small tables. Nothing tests capacity-limited single-provider services.

findings.summary: Share changes appear mostly as penetration changes with small loyalty changes. Unusual loyalty does not predict future growth. Growing and declining brands lose customers at roughly the rate their size predicts; what differs is acquisition.
findings.limitations: Correlational, brand-level evidence. Mature-category bias.

findings.summary: Track brand metrics quarterly rather than annually, because quarterly data matches the pace of marketing changes.
findings.limitations: Advice for panel-tracked brands. Small businesses may have too few buyers per quarter for stable rates.

findings.summary: Exceptions to double jeopardy usually come from restricted penetration (regional distribution, store brands, a genuine niche) or change-of-pace/occasion brands. The authors advise looking first for distribution or penetration impediments when loyalty looks unusual. They describe niche brands as having limited growth potential.
findings.limitations: The 'pity niche brands' view assumes scale is the goal. That doesn't hold for a capacity-limited owner-operator.

findings.summary: First National Bank (South Africa), an institute sponsor, switched from cross-selling to a penetration strategy. Reported customers rose from 5.8m to 7.5m (+29%) while products per customer moved from 2.03 to 2.1 (+3%).
findings.limitations: Sponsor case told by the authors. No counterfactual.

findings.summary: Remove self-inflicted penetration barriers: entry price (small packs in Thailand haircare), missing variants, category complexity (wine), fear of fakes.
findings.limitations: Examples are consumer goods.

findings.summary: Heavy-buyer fallacy: heavy buyers are few and already buy the brand a lot, so there is little headroom. In one institute study of business clients who left their financial-services provider, about 60% of defection was beyond marketers' influence and only 4% was due to a service issue.
findings.limitations: Defection split comes from one study (Bogomolova & Romaniuk 2009) whose sample isn't described here.

findings.summary: Most word of mouth comes from lighter buyers because there are so many of them. In the Indonesian department-store example, the 11% heavier shoppers gave 15% of the word of mouth.
findings.limitations: Single retailer survey.

findings.summary: Purchase-frequency distributions follow a reverse-J (negative binomial) shape everywhere tested. Growth mainly shrinks the zero-buyer group, and growing brands gain more light buyers than heavy ones.
findings.limitations: Requires buyer-level data over a fixed period.

findings.summary: The Pareto share is nearer 50:20 than 80:20: the top 20% of a brand's buyers account for about 40-60% of annual sales. The emerging-market table averages about 53%.
findings.limitations: Repeat consumer categories. B2B and agency revenue can be far more concentrated, and the book doesn't test that.

findings.summary: About half of one period's heaviest buyers aren't heavy in the next period (regression to the mean). So a snapshot classification of 'VIP' customers misclassifies many of them. Malaysian top-20% stability averages were about 39% for soap and 48% for noodles.
findings.limitations: Table rows OCR'd unreliably; only averages and the prose 'about half' are used.

findings.summary: Natural monopoly law: big brands' customer bases contain more light category buyers. Small brands' customers buy more other brands (Russian fast food: McDonald's customers bought about 2.6 other brands versus about 5.6 for Sbarro).
findings.limitations: Effect is described as modest. Chart values partly garbled; the two figures cited also appear in prose.

findings.summary: Sole loyalty is rare among heavy category buyers and highest among very infrequent buyers. Even in banking, holding a second product roughly halves the share of solely loyal customers.
findings.limitations: Survey-based.

findings.summary: Practise sophisticated mass marketing: cover buyer variety with a product range and point-of-sale options, not by targeting segments. Don't target more narrowly than category buyers. Treating the market as one persona is dangerous. Quorn moved from vegetarian substitute (about 7% of UK households relevant) to healthy eating (about 70%).
findings.limitations: Quorn and Goya are self-reported company cases. The guidance concerns brand reach, not sales prioritisation in B2B.

findings.summary: Competing brands sell to similar customer profiles. In fast food across 11 emerging markets, only 2.5% of brands deviated by more than 10 points on any characteristic (over 3,000 cross-tabs). Larger differences in banking had functional causes: product range, fees, branch locations.
findings.limitations: PDF p.64 OCR conf 0.83 (table values not used). Demographic profiles only.

findings.summary: Duplication of purchase law: a brand shares customers with each rival in line with that rival's penetration. Deviations (partitions) are flagged at roughly 10 points as a rule of thumb. Common causes are the same owner, functional sub-markets (e.g. diet drinks) and a small sibling's distribution gaps. The analysis period must be long enough to reveal repertoires but not so long that everything overlaps.
findings.limitations: Needs buyer-level data on several brands. Small businesses rarely have it.

findings.summary: When a brand behaves differently, check incomplete distribution and functional differences before positioning explanations. Local brands are not a separate sub-market; their threat follows their share.

Current users give far more brand associations than non-users, about 2-3 times as many. The cross-study average is roughly 48% for current buyers, 19% for former and 10% for never-buyers. This holds even for negative-sounding attributes such as 'expensive'.
findings.limitations: Average row read from a partly garbled table; it matches the 1970 averages quoted (50/20/10).

findings.summary: Category entry points (CEPs) are the pre-brand cues buyers use to retrieve options: needs, occasions, places, company, pairings. They are generated with why, when, where, with whom and with what. Mental availability is how broadly and freshly the brand links to the CEPs that matter. Large brands link to more CEPs, so breadth beats owning one or two.
findings.limitations: Evidence is cross-sectional (big brands have more links). Causal direction is partly reversed by F18.

findings.summary: Mental availability metrics from a CEP-by-brand grid: mental market share (brand's CEP links over all brands' links), mental penetration (share of category buyers linking the brand to at least one CEP) and network size (CEPs linked among those linking any). A single 'would you consider' question is outdated because evoked sets depend on context. CEP relevance can be ranked by how often CEPs are linked to any brand.
findings.limitations: The book gives no minimum sample size or CEP count. The India handset example uses 16 CEPs.

findings.summary: Treat positioning as the temporary result of current advertised messages. Each execution carries one clear CEP, and campaigns rotate CEPs over time. Ask which CEP an execution builds, how common it is, and when it was last promoted.
findings.limitations: Advertising-centred. Small businesses mostly use posts, listings and pages, but the same test applies (the authors' footnote says all marketing activity).

findings.summary: Explicit brand rejection is low (institute testing across 500+ brands, 24 categories, 23 countries), so lack of mental availability matters more than rejection. Attitude scales with no 'no opinion' option inflate attitudes, and brand love is rare and of little consequence.
findings.limitations: Per-country rejection values in Fig 4.6 are garbled and not used.

findings.summary: Distinctive assets are non-name brand elements (colour, logo, character, sound, font, tagline, shape) that trigger the brand. Distinctiveness (how you're recognised and found) is separate from differentiation (why you're bought). Strength is measured by fame (share of category buyers linking the asset to the brand) and uniqueness (share of the asset's brand links that go to this brand). A grid at 50/50 gives four quadrants: Use or Lose, Investable, Avoid solo use, Ignore or Test.
findings.limitations: Proprietary method (Romaniuk & Nenycz-Thiel 2014). The full survey protocol isn't in the book.

findings.summary: Build assets with three steps: reach category buyers, show the asset prominently together with the name, and stay consistent. Check consistency by laying out all collateral together. For variants, keep the parent assets and add a variant twist. Don't base assets on meaning or the current positioning. Avoid pack changes. Pick a varied palette (colour, shape, a face, a sound if audio is used, a short phrase), starting with one or two that work on pack and at the start of ads. Measure assets, because managers overrate them.
findings.limitations: Most examples are large packaged-goods brands.

findings.summary: Online, branding through visually rich distinctive assets gave online ads more cut-through than name-only branding, and images beat taglines. The authors describe the optimal online design as a visually rich image with a unique link to the brand name. Assets must stay legible at the small sizes used in online shops.
findings.limitations: Cites institute theses (Major 2014; Hartnett 2011) without detail.

findings.summary: A 2015 asset test (online samples of n=300 per country in the USA, China, Brazil and South Africa) found the same brand's asset strength varied by country, e.g. some fast-food logos usable in the USA but only investable elsewhere.
findings.limitations: Grid charts garbled; only prose highlights used.

findings.summary: Reach is the primary media objective. Their worked example: of 1,000 people, 60% reach at a 5% response gives 30 sales. Lower reach needs a much higher response for the same sales (7.5% at 40% reach, 10% at 30%, 30% at 10%).
findings.limitations: Assumes response rate doesn't rise when targeting narrows. That is precisely what targeting advocates dispute.

findings.summary: Within a period, the first exposure has the largest effect, and the 'frequency of three' rule is a myth. Bursts over-hit heavy media users. Continuous presence beats matching competitors' bursts unless sales are highly seasonal.
findings.limitations: Single-source TV-era evidence (Taylor, Kennedy & Sharp 2009).

findings.summary: With a small budget, don't trade reach for 'engagement' (high cost per contact). A small brand's real limit is often physical availability. Advertise where you sell, and use regional media when distribution is regional.
findings.limitations: Doesn't address platform minimum spends or search-based demand capture.

findings.summary: Media and platform use follows double jeopardy, so smaller platforms' audiences are heavier media users who are also on the big ones. Add a medium only if it adds more unduplicated than duplicated reach, and prefer mixing media families. Formats that make people work for exposure (fan pages, events) reach mostly heavy brand buyers.
findings.limitations: Platform lists are from 2014-15.

findings.summary: In a 2012 personal-care survey across Asian emerging markets, pack on shelf, TV, flyers, price promotions and gifts with purchase reached the most category buyers. Social, mobile and internet ads ranked lowest.
findings.limitations: One category, 2012; digital rankings are likely outdated.

findings.summary: Positive word of mouth is about 2-5 times (typically about 3 times) more common than negative, and the impact per instance is similar. In a 2014 China survey, 85% of word of mouth came from colleagues, family and friends. Current users give most positive WOM and lapsed users most negative. NPS misses defectors' negative WOM. WOM volume tracks market share.
findings.limitations: Mostly conversational WOM. Public online reviews aren't analysed separately.

findings.summary: Positive WOM moves low-propensity recipients most, but most recipients are already likely buyers. In US cars, the average lift was +0.9 points, 63% of recipients already had a 70%+ prior, and impact at 70-80% prior was about 0.4. Negative WOM is the reverse. No evidence was found that WOM has more impact in China than in the USA.
findings.limitations: Self-reported before/after purchase probabilities.

findings.summary: WOM also reinforces the giver's own memory. Conversation-worthy stories travel beyond in-market people, and fresh stories are needed because people don't repeat a story. New brands can't rely on WOM because few people have experience of them. Heavy WOM investment at the expense of controllable media is risky.

Physical availability has three parts: presence (are you where buying happens), relevance (are you buyable: range, sizes, price points, payment) and prominence (are you easy to find). Mental and physical availability must overlap. The authors suggest launching in one region with regional media, and starting broad advertising slightly before rollout.

Shoppers add channels rather than switch; average channel share loyalty was about 30% in four emerging markets. Retailers and channels show double jeopardy and duplication patterns. Small outlets' shoppers also shop at big ones. Accessibility, more than shopper type, drives who uses a channel (the Soweto mall example).
findings.limitations: Urban internet-panel samples, 2012-14.

findings.summary: For services, separate sales channels from servicing channels. Cutting branches moves transactions online but hurts acquisition: a Bain 2013 report cited by the authors showed branches still dominated new account openings in most of 27 countries. Easy-to-find branches, phone numbers and websites keep a mentally available service from slipping off the list.
findings.limitations: Banking only. Online acquisition has grown since 2013.

findings.summary: Relevance means designing for buying occasions, not segments: cover high-volume variants, growing sub-markets and partitions without over-investing in a niche. Remove barriers through pack/size range, price-point variety, payment options such as instalments, and non-product barriers (income insecurity, congestion, lack of banking).
findings.limitations: Emerging-market examples.

findings.summary: Prominence: be distinctive, not odd. Gimmicky or frequently changed packs slow recognition, because shoppers screen out what they aren't looking for.

Online: double jeopardy holds for brands and e-retailers, and brand share loyalty is higher online (UK 2013, dog food 21% offline vs 33% online). The authors found no consistent small-brand advantage online. About two-thirds of a grocer's online buyers are its offline shoppers. More than half of online purchases take about 13 seconds, and abandoning a basket is easy.
findings.limitations: UK and US grocery panels, 2013-14; marketplaces and social commerce not covered.

findings.summary: Decide on an online presence by the shopping occasions you'd miss and by the country's and category's e-commerce maturity. Start with part of the range that people are comfortable buying online and that benefits from delivery. New grocery brands may break into repertoires more easily offline. Being online is no excuse to cut advertising.
findings.limitations: Grocery-centred.

findings.summary: New brands' metrics settle to normal for their share quickly, and they grow through penetration. First buyers skew to heavy category buyers, who mostly become light buyers of the new brand. New brands show slightly lower loyalty than similar-share established brands, which the authors attribute to temporarily bought availability and discounts. Six in ten recent new Coke Zero buyers held fewer than 3 of 18 associations.
findings.limitations: Consumer goods. Assumes the product was pre-tested; the authors say rejection is rarely the cause of failure.

findings.summary: Two-stage launch. Stage 1: wide reach to secure distribution and first sales, with minimal frequency. Stage 2: stay on air for medium and light buyers. Priority memories are what the brand is, what it looks like and where to buy it. Favour common CEPs over a rare 'ownable' one. Make branding early, frequent, spaced out and both visual and audio. Borrow existing cultural memory structures (Snickers linked to tiffin in India). Run a rejection check with neutral wording.

Use the duplication law as the cannibalisation benchmark for a new variant or second brand. Fix excess overlap by widening the smaller brand's distribution and building its own mental availability, not by targeting different people. Deliberately accepting high cannibalisation can be a choice made to block a competitor.
findings.limitations: The benchmark needs overlap data with other brands.

findings.summary: Luxury brands behave like normal brands. Awareness correlated with ownership (about 0.9) and with desirability (about 0.8-0.9). Owners rated their brand more desirable than aware non-owners did (clothing 17% vs 12%, champagne 22% vs 14%, watches 13.4% vs 13.3%). Perceived restricted distribution didn't go with perceived exclusivity. Duplication and natural monopoly laws hold. Most luxury sales come from the middle class.
findings.limitations: Online samples in Russia, the USA and China (2015). The authors call it a first exploration.

findings.summary: In emerging markets the same laws hold. Start distribution with modern trade, then decide on nano stores, your own route to market or e-commerce by country and category. Distinctive assets help low-literacy buyers and shopkeepers find brands.
findings.limitations: Large-brand distribution context; little direct relevance to most ClimbOS users.

findings.summary: A good metric is comparative (over time, across groups), understandable, usually a ratio or rate, and changes what you do. The action for each outcome should be agreed before the data come in.
findings.limitations: Rules of thumb, not a formal metric theory.

findings.summary: Vanity metrics are numbers you cannot act on. Cumulative counts (total signups, total active users) only go up; the actionable version is a rate such as share of users active. The book lists eight common ones: hits, page views, visits, unique visitors, followers/likes, time on site, emails collected, downloads.
findings.limitations: The book itself says page views and uniques are real revenue metrics for ad-funded media (BK12-F23).

findings.summary: Five distinctions to keep in mind: qualitative vs quantitative, vanity vs actionable, exploratory vs reporting, leading vs lagging, correlated vs causal. Early on, measure lagging metrics; leading indicators need cohort comparisons first.
findings.limitations: Causality is discussed informally; Book 03 and BK06 cover it rigorously.

findings.summary: Metrics come in pairs that together drive a fundamental number: conversion with time to purchase, viral coefficient with cycle time.

HighScore House set an MVP 'active family' line of 4 uses a week, missed it, called both churned and light users, found a segment getting value at 1-2 uses a week, and lowered the line. The authors allow moving a line only when qualitative evidence shows a segment's real usage, never to get over it.
findings.limitations: Single case, reported by the authors' own accelerator.

findings.summary: Segments are groups sharing a trait; cohorts are groups that started at the same time and are compared at the same age. A blended average can look flat while each new cohort performs better (the book's hypothetical retailer table).
findings.limitations: Teaching example with invented numbers.

findings.summary: Be data-informed, not purely data-driven: optimisation finds local maxima within a known design; people must propose new designs. Common data pitfalls include unclean data, not normalising, ignoring seasonality, ignoring base size when reporting growth, data vomit and over-sensitive alerts.
findings.limitations: Pitfall list is one data scientist's, reported.

findings.summary: Circle of Friends (2008) found through exploratory segmentation that mothers engaged far more than other users and pivoted to Circle of Moms; numbers initially fell, then engaged usage grew.
findings.limitations: Facebook-platform era; survivorship.

findings.summary: Five stages, Empathy, Stickiness, Virality, Revenue, Scale, each with a qualitative 'gate' to pass before moving on: a real, poorly met need in a reachable market; a solution people will adopt and pay for; a product that keeps users; users and features that fuel growth; a sustainable business with the right margins. Follow the order unless you have a really good reason not to.
findings.limitations: Gates are statements, not numbers; figure alignment from OCR is uncertain. Authors admit the model is prescriptive and was criticised.

findings.summary: Turning on paid acquisition before the product is sticky (and ideally viral) is usually premature; virality is a force multiplier for paid spend, which is why it precedes Revenue and Scale.
findings.limitations: The authors' footnote (p182) says a good business builds all three engines; the order is about focus, not exclusion.

findings.summary: One Metric That Matters: at any time, one number tied to the riskiest question for your current stage gets priority; others are still tracked. It changes as you move stages and becomes harder to keep single once a company scales.
findings.limitations: Taken alone it can hide harm; the book's 'metrics come in pairs' and squeeze-toy ideas partly cover guardrails.

findings.summary: Lines in the sand have two legitimate sources: what your business model needs (preferred), or, when the model is still unknown, what is normal for similar businesses.
findings.limitations: 'Normal' from 2013 aggregates is weak evidence for a 2026 small business.

findings.summary: Squeeze toy: optimising the current metric exposes the next constraint (enrolments → cost per customer; traffic → conversion).

A San Diego restaurant tracks daily staff cost as a share of revenue (about 24% judged right; above 30% bad; under 20% risks under-serving) and 5 p.m. reservations as a leading indicator of covers (about 5:1 for that restaurant).
findings.limitations: One restaurant's ratios; the owner says they differ by restaurant type.

findings.summary: Not all users are good: some pay late, some only market for you, some cost you. Segment real users from drive-bys; freemium is a selling tactic, not a business model.

Kevin Hillstrom's e-commerce modes by annual repurchase rate: acquisition mode below 40%, hybrid 40-60%, loyalty above 60%; early proxy by 90-day repurchase: 1-15%, 15-30%, above 30%. He reports most mature e-commerce businesses (about 70%) are in acquisition mode, about 10% in loyalty mode, that the annual rate rarely moves more than about 10% relative, and that loyalty pushes in acquisition mode don't work.
findings.limitations: One consultant's client experience, circa 2012; no sample size. Never a ClimbOS threshold.

findings.summary: In e-commerce, conversion, repeat purchases and order size multiply into revenue per customer, the better single health metric; optimise revenue per visitor, not conversion alone (WineExpress test: 41% more revenue per visitor).
findings.limitations: WineExpress is an agency-reported single test.

findings.summary: SaaS should usually focus on stickiness first, acquiring only enough attention to test it; some metrics can't be measured until earlier ones exist (no conversion without users), so de-risk in order.
Backupify (2010) paid $243 to acquire a consumer paying $39 a year, pivoted to businesses, later reported CLV:CAC of 5-6x and a target payback of 12 months or less per channel.
findings.limitations: Venture-funded company; self-reported.

findings.summary: Churn = churned customers in a period / customers at the start; simple average lifetime = 1 / monthly churn (2.5% gives 40 months). With fast or uneven growth, start-of-period and averaged denominators mislead; measure by cohort or over very short periods. Track unpaid and paid churn separately; treat 90 days without login as churned.
findings.limitations: Simple lifetime formula assumes constant churn; Guide 04 and Book 12 prefer cohort survival.

findings.summary: ClearFit moved from $99/month to $350 per job posting; sales tripled and revenue rose about tenfold because buyers hire sporadically and compared it with job-board pricing.
findings.limitations: Self-reported, single case.

findings.summary: Free mobile apps: track ARPU and ARPPU separately because few 'whales' pay most; check churn at 1 day, 1 week and 1 month since each points to a different cause (onboarding, depth, update cadence).
findings.limitations: App-store mechanics described are 2012-era.

findings.summary: For ad-funded media, many 'vanity' numbers (uniques, page views, time on site) are the inventory that earns revenue. Audience churn can be estimated as new visitors minus net change in uniques; a campaign can hide churn.
findings.limitations: Inventory still needs pairing with revenue per impression.

findings.summary: UGC sites manage an engagement funnel (lurk, vote, comment, post, create groups) and should compare tier conversion by monthly cohort; a small minority creates most content.

Two-sided marketplaces: focus on the side with money (usually buyers), seed the other side by hand, measure liquidity (searches returning at least one result, buyer:seller ratio, active listings) and satisfied transactions, and fight leakage. Long-term you can buy supply but not demand.
findings.limitations: Game-console example tables are invented.

findings.summary: Empathy stage: talk to at least 15 people at each interviewing stage; positive signals are wanting to pay now, already trying to solve it, and offering follow-ups and referrals. An optional scoring rubric (six questions, maximum 43 points, 31 or more counted as good) helps compare interviews and spot segments.
findings.limitations: Scores and the 31 cut-off are the authors' arbitrary choices; body-language items are subjective.

findings.summary: 'Good enough' incumbents and inertia beat slightly better products; check how people solve it today. Size markets top-down and bottom-up and compare.
findings.limitations: The '10 times better' line is rhetoric, not data.

findings.summary: For surveys and answers-at-scale: decide what a good score is before sending, put segmentation questions first and open questions last, test with three target people, and track cost per completed response.
findings.limitations: Paid recruitment tools named are dated.

findings.summary: Before building an MVP, name its OMTM and success line; at this point acquisition volume is irrelevant; narrow the test (one area, one category); every feature needs a usage metric; remove unused features.

To leave Stickiness you must show people use the product as expected and get enough value; do not drive new traffic until you can turn attention into engagement. Exception: products that need a critical mass (listings, nearby drivers) must seed it first.

Premature virality and scaling waste acquired users who churn; ask seven questions before building a feature (why it helps retention, measurable, build time, complexity, risk, innovation, what users say vs do).

Virality comes in three kinds (inherent, artificial/incentivised, word of mouth) that bring different user quality and should be segmented. Viral coefficient = invites per user x acceptance rate; cycle time matters as much. For enterprise, net promoter score and references stand in for click-to-invite virality. A sustained coefficient above 1 is rare.
findings.limitations: NPS is a weak proxy, as the book concedes.

findings.summary: Good leading indicators come early in the lifecycle, tie to the business model, and are found by comparing cohorts or segments that stayed vs left; causation must be tested before using one as a lever. Reported examples (Facebook friends in first days, Zynga next-day return, Dropbox first file) are 2012 anecdotes.
findings.limitations: Examples are conference anecdotes; ClimbOS should not import those thresholds.

findings.summary: Charging from the start is fine and common; the Revenue stage is about shifting focus to margins, pricing and reinvesting in acquisition. Revenue per customer is a better health ratio than raw revenue.

SaaS 'magic number' (attributed to Josh James, 2008): change in quarterly recurring revenue divided by the previous quarter's sales and marketing spend; below 0.75 signals a problem, above 1 signals room to invest.
findings.limitations: The prose says 'annual recurring revenue' but the printed formula uses quarterly values without annualising; definitions in the wider literature differ, so the thresholds depend on the variant.

findings.summary: Choose which 'more' to pull by model: efficiency for per-transaction costs, more people when viral, more often for loyal buyers, more money for one-off big tickets, more stuff (upsell) for subscriptions fighting churn.

CLV must exceed CAC with room for operations, and cash timing matters because you pay to acquire up front. Breakeven gates before Scale: breakeven on variable costs, time to customer breakeven (book example: $27 over 11 months, $14 CAC, about 5.7 months), EBITDA breakeven, and 'hibernation' (survive with no new marketing).
findings.limitations: Book's example is hypothetical.

findings.summary: When traction stalls, try a new market for the existing product before building features (market/product fit); 'SMBs' is not a market, narrow by industry, geography, buying process and budget.

At Scale, compare payback and churn by channel, region and campaign; watch for falling engagement, saturation and rising CAC. Keep three big assumptions, three weekly actions and three daily experiments aligned (Three-Threes).

Buffer charged from launch because the founder needed revenue to quit his job, used revenue as proof of stickiness, checked churn (target under 5%, actual about 2%) before shifting to acquisition, and kept watching conversion of each new channel.
findings.limitations: Self-reported; 2012.

findings.summary: Growth rate (Paul Graham, Y Combinator, c. 2012): 5-7% a week good, 10% exceptional, 1% a sign the team hasn't figured it out; authors' line: 5% weekly in active users pre-revenue, 5% weekly revenue after.
findings.limitations: Accelerator context over a few weeks; the authors themselves call it B2C-biased and warn growth before fit can kill a company.

findings.summary: B2B growth differs: early customers treat you like consultants; growing prematurely can alienate the core customers whose references you need.
Fred Wilson's 30/10/10 (2011): about 30% of registered users use a web service monthly, 10% daily, peak concurrency 10% of daily users.
findings.limitations: One VC portfolio; consumer web.

findings.summary: Cross-model 2012-2013 lines: monthly churn under 5% (ideally 2%) = reasonably sticky, while Startup Compass averages were 12-19%; consumer apps near 1:1 CAC:CLV; spend no more than a third of CLV on acquisition (book calls it widely cited, not a hard rule); viral coefficient above 0.75 'pretty good'; email 20-30% open and over 5% click; 99.5% uptime for relied-on paid services; about 1 minute engaged time per page; pages under 5 seconds.
findings.limitations: Mixed sources, mostly vendor or VC claims; email open rates are now distorted by privacy proxies.

findings.summary: E-commerce (2007-2012 sources): startups should expect about 2% conversion (1-3%), 10% is exceptional; cart abandonment about 65%; one seller doubled conversion from 5% to 10% by folding $5 shipping into a $35 price.
findings.limitations: Vertical spread is large (0.4%-5.8% by category in the cited table).

findings.summary: Totango data (100+ SaaS companies, c. 2012): card required at signup, 0.5-2% of visitors start a trial and 40-50% convert; no card, 5-10% start and about 15% convert; first-bill churn up to 40% with a card, up to 20% without; end to end about 0.6% vs 1.2%. Targeting 'serious evaluators' (said to be 20% of visitors) lifted the book's example to 2%.
findings.limitations: The book's 'bottom line' says a 40% increase, but its own table goes from 60 to 100 customers (67%); treat the summary sentence as unreliable.

findings.summary: SaaS (2009-2012): best companies 1.5-3% monthly churn; get under 5% before scaling (Mark MacLeod), with a path under 2% to scale far (David Skok); best-in-class grow revenue per customer about 20% a year; about 2.3% of subscribers move up a tier and about 0.6% of free users start paying in a month (Price Intelligently); Evernote under 1% paid after month one rising to about 12% after two years.
findings.limitations: Venture-backed SaaS samples; not small-business SaaS.

findings.summary: Free mobile apps (2012): paid installs $0.10-0.70, in-app ad installs $1.50-4.00, blended target $0.50-0.75; up to 80% day-one drop; Flurry 54/43/35% of users left after months 1/2/3; about 2% of freemium users pay and 1.5% of game players buy; ARPDAU above $0.05; under 1.5% review rate for paid apps, well under 1% for free.
findings.limitations: App-store economics and paid-install practices have changed; several tactics described may now breach store rules.

findings.summary: Media (2010-2012): on-page ads 0.5-2% CTR, below 0.08% (blank-ad noise) means something is wrong; about 5% of clicks never land; content pages should hold about 90 seconds engaged time; median views per share about 9 on Facebook.

UGC (2010-2012): about 17 minutes a day on site signals stickiness; authors' estimate 25% lurk, 60-70% take easy core actions, 5-15% create, with 80% of content from a small group; reddit reported spam at about half of submissions in 2011.
findings.limitations: Participation norms vary by country and platform (the book's own BBC/GWI tables).

findings.summary: Without an external baseline, plot your own improvement curve; when gains flatten toward an asymptote, that is your practical baseline and a signal to change metric or strategy. Move your ability to the line, not the line to your ability.
findings.limitations: Ch 28's recap restates churn 'below 2.5%', inconsistent with the 5%/2% lines elsewhere.

findings.summary: Enterprise differences: customer development is a census of a few buyers, not a poll; buyers and users differ; legacy systems and incumbents slow change; cycle times are longer; the main stickiness risk is integration; consulting-led starts risk staying consultancies; segment by vertical or region.
findings.limitations: Written for venture-scale enterprise software.

findings.summary: Enterprise metrics: ease of getting meetings, documented sales-stage conversion, integration and support cost per customer, real usage (logins can be mandated, so measure productivity), client baselines captured before deployment to prove ROI, disentangling anchor customers, profitability by customer (a cited study: top 20% of customers 150-300% of profits), discrete-choice roadmap questions, and channel pitch baselines.
findings.limitations: The profitability split is from a 2001 cost-management study cited second-hand.

findings.summary: Intrapreneurs add a step zero (executive sponsor, agreed lines in the sand) and should sell the business model with analytics after launch rather than a predicted business case.
findings.limitations: Low relevance to ClimbOS's owner-operators.

findings.summary: qidiq let invitees answer a survey before creating an account; response rates rose from 10-25% to 70-90%, and the team dropped its planned mobile app.
findings.limitations: Year One Labs portfolio company; self-reported.

findings.summary: Pricing: the book's elasticity table peaks at $660 revenue at both $11 and $12; it suggests pricing about 10% below the revenue peak to favour adoption (a founder's rule echoed from Zoosk) and cites a 133-company survey where only 18-21% used customer research or sensitivity tests to price.
findings.limitations: Elasticity table is hypothetical; the '10% below' rule is opinion.

findings.summary: Conversion rate is the share of visitors reaching a stated goal; the 'content' can be any message or interface (checkout, email, sales script, packaging) and the goal is whatever the content exists to do, not always a sale.
findings.limitations: Broad definition; does not address metric choice trade-offs.

findings.summary: A/B testing measures but does not generate ideas; what you put into a test decides its value (the stopwatch, not the sprinter). Testing lets you discard missteps and postpone hard decisions until data arrive.
findings.limitations: Claim that iterative testing means profit 'can only go up' ignores false positives, novelty and regression to the mean.

findings.summary: A telecom client tested its current handset price against free; free did not sell more because buyers suspected a catch, so the team tested higher-priced premium versions and upsells instead and won.
findings.limitations: Single client, no numbers, no stats reported.

findings.summary: Power Law of CRO: revenue = visitors x conversion x customer spend; because ad and fixed costs do not scale with conversion, profit rises more than proportionally, and the extra profit lets a business bid more for traffic (a virtuous circle).
findings.limitations: Diagrams are images. Assumes extra traffic is buyable at similar quality and that fixed costs truly stay fixed; the authors say to model your own numbers.

findings.summary: Doubling end-to-end conversion needs only about a 19% gain at each of four stages (1.19^4 = 2.005), and a 19% page gain needs about 1.76% from each of ten elements (1.0176^10 = 1.19).
findings.limitations: Arithmetic is correct but assumes independent, multiplicative stage effects; small element gains are exactly what the meek-tweaking chapter says cannot be detected.

findings.summary: Scientific Web Design: design for function over aesthetics, measure changes experimentally, and change often in small targeted iterations rather than big redesigns, to minimise work-in-progress.
findings.limitations: Redesign failure claims (e.g. nine in ten redesigns go wrong, part0070 [276]) are the agency's own observation, not a study.

findings.summary: Meek tweaking (button colours, shuffling, copying others' wins) fails because small effects take disproportionately long to detect: at 300 page views a day an 80% lift reads in about 2 days, 20% in about 23 days, 10% in several months. Aim for bold, targeted changes.
findings.limitations: Baseline rate and test settings are in the unreadable graph. My check: a ~10% baseline at 80% power and 5% alpha reproduces 1.5 / 24 / 96 days. A 2-day test breaks the whole-week rule used elsewhere in the library.

findings.summary: DiPS (Diagnose, Problem, Solution): find out why visitors do not act before choosing a remedy. Each objection has a matching counter (don't know what it does: explain; don't see why: benefits; doubt it works: proof; compatibility: details; too expensive: justify price; distrust company: credibility; will think about it: reasons to act now). Unmatched remedies only add clutter.
findings.limitations: Diagnosis is still inference; the book offers no rule for ranking several concurrent problems.

findings.summary: Every mechanism has a specific function: guarantees reduce risk and act as proof, so they help only when risk or credibility is the issue; negative headlines work only when the reader has decided to act and fears choosing wrongly.
findings.limitations: Reported from agency experience.

findings.summary: Low-traffic sites face two problems: too few visitors to learn from and too few to measure with. Techniques that work at a few visitors a day: user tests (most fruitful), watching session recordings, talking to people who sell the product face to face, studying competitors or adjacent businesses, adding a prominent phone number, and raising survey incentives.
findings.limitations: No traffic thresholds given for when other methods become viable.

findings.summary: Some surveys typically get about a 3% completion rate; pop-up invitations to user tests with an incentive get about 5% response, varying widely by industry (finance and health lower).
findings.limitations: Agency figures from ~2017, no sample described. Use the owner's own rate when known.

findings.summary: Use web analytics early to find the high-traffic flows ('arteries') worth working on: changing a page nobody visits, or one already converting fully, does nothing. Analytics shows where, never why.

Behaviour tools: click maps reveal clicks on non-links and false bottoms (look for anomalies, not the predictable heat); session recordings show struggle and errors; form analytics show field-level drop-off, time, blanks and errors.
findings.limitations: Tool names dated; privacy consent and PII masking not discussed.

findings.summary: Live chat transcripts and refined canned responses are tested counter-objection copy; knowledge bases and site-search logs reveal what visitors cannot find and their own words.

Ask buyers 'What nearly stopped you buying from us?' Buyers are qualified, went through the whole funnel and remember the barriers; non-buyers are a mixed group whose answers (often price) can mislead. Other useful survey themes: alternatives considered, why they chose you, what would make them use you more, NPS.
findings.limitations: Survivorship: buyers cannot report barriers that stopped everyone else; pair with observation of non-buyers.

findings.summary: Exit surveys: ask the visit purpose, whether it was achieved, and if not, what stopped them; add a segment question where segments differ. On-page surveys can target the moment and visitor type.
findings.limitations: Need traffic to yield enough answers.

findings.summary: Ultra-qualitative methods give empathy that numbers and surveys cannot: method marketing (become a customer, including buying, unboxing, using; offline analogues often solved onboarding better), selling face to face, phone calls, and VOC aggregators (salespeople, support, resellers who already know buyers and the relative weight of issues).
findings.limitations: Time-intensive; risk of over-weighting the researcher's own experience (one customer).

findings.summary: When selling face to face for research, try to close for real: people asked for 'market research' give polite, false answers, while a real sales attempt surfaces true objections. Log objections and the counters that worked in a two-column sheet.
findings.limitations: Ethics: only sell what can be delivered; collecting names needs consent.

findings.summary: Good salespeople carry decision trees; map them into on-site choice flows rather than listing product codes.
findings.limitations: Reported 214% order increase is a client case.

findings.summary: User tests: give a realistic task, stay silent, ask thoughts, record. Start with whoever is at hand (hallway), move to target users when easy problems are gone, and use retrospective walkthroughs with people who just bought. Less web-savvy users reveal more. Rarely more than three tests pass without a major idea.
findings.limitations: 'Three tests' is agency experience; recruitment via pop-ups is self-selected (part0049 [43]).

findings.summary: Low-traffic measurement: test big bold changes, use earlier (micro) conversions, test only pages most buyers see, apply one change across similar pages in one test, consider ending at 90% or even 85% confidence, use a fixed maximum duration then decide, temporarily buy traffic, and if every test would exceed about six months, use user tests only until the business grows.
findings.limitations: Lower confidence and 'promote the challenger if research-driven' conflict with the library's fixed-horizon and causal-wording rules unless pre-registered and labelled directional.

findings.summary: Most websites underperform in a small set of recurring ways (the book names fourteen chapters): unclear writing, poor usability, not offering what visitors want, unclear benefits, weak offer, low trust, risk, not ready to buy, complexity, competitors, lost attention, delay, a handover outside your control, low lifetime value. Use research to find which applies, then go to that fix.
findings.limitations: Taxonomy is the agency's, not validated; categories overlap.

findings.summary: Clear writing is a prerequisite to all persuasion: run readability tests with a real reader, record yourself selling then edit the transcript, keep sentences short, reach the verb fast, cut fluff, replace nominalisations, put the key point at the end.
findings.limitations: Memory-buffer '15 words' is an illustrative claim, not cited.

findings.summary: Usability: designers suffer the curse of knowledge; prototype in low fidelity (wireframes), test on one or two people, iterate. Preference tests give opinions that may not predict behaviour.
findings.limitations: Tool lists dated.

findings.summary: Visitor-intention gap analysis: after at least 100 on-page answers to 'what did you come here to do', group intentions, record each share, whether you satisfy it, how you could monetise it and the revenue it could earn; explore new lines by low-risk steps (refer or advertise others first, then build).
findings.limitations: Suggests a temporary AdSense box as an idea source; that harms user experience and brand and is dated. Revenue estimates in column 5 are assumptions.

findings.summary: Features vs benefits is a function choice: if readers say 'so what?', add the benefit; if they say 'yeah, right', add the feature or other proof. Plain description beats brand slogans, unmentioned included value is common, and a 'what happens after you say yes' process diagram (future pacing) helps services.
findings.limitations: Mobal/Moz outcomes are reported cases.

findings.summary: Offer levers: decide what to monetise; penetration pricing with economies of scale, skimming without; lead with a no-brainer first purchase that is the most-liked product; free trials or simulations; installments when research shows cash constraints; good/better/best and a 10x tier; premiums; a stated reason for any deal; payment methods and minimum terms; test prices fairly.
findings.limitations: Several tactics (strike-through was-prices, rolling time-limited offers, odd prices, decimal display) carry legal or trust risk and weak evidence today.

findings.summary: Trust: show proof that already exists ('proof magnets': reviews, press, partners, data) on high-traffic pages; then invest in acquiring the proof visitors find most persuasive. Trust in the company and trust in the product are separate problems.
findings.limitations: Celebrity example notes one celebrity reduced sales, so test before committing.

findings.summary: Guarantees work when buyers want the promise, fear the risk or doubt the claim, and the product delivers. Name it, word it positively, match its type to the concern (performance, satisfaction, price-match), make it easy to invoke, refund promptly, place it where risk is felt. Roll out by scenario-modelling uplift x invocation rate, a short test, waiting out the claim period, then computing net profit.
findings.limitations: Invocation 'often an order of magnitude lower than expected' is agency experience. Statutory rights must not be presented as a special guarantee in some jurisdictions.

findings.summary: Most visitors are not ready to buy; build a multistep funnel where each step offers an attractive reward (guides, tools, community, email course) until the buyer is ready. Readiness follows triggers (contract ends, a move, a project start); be remembered or appear inside other companies' funnels at that time.
findings.limitations: Funnel Planner columns are images; MoneySavingExpert sale figures are historical.

findings.summary: Complex sales: keep an objection/counter-objection (O/CO) table ranked by frequency; reduce the commitment of the next step, then use as many words as a face-to-face sale would need; offer dual paths; organise copy into labelled modules (separation of concerns); keep headings within about three levels; navigation in the buyer's mental model; spoiler or teaser headings instead of category labels; progressive disclosure on the page rather than separate pages; fallbacks (search, knowledge base, chat, phone).
findings.limitations: Hover triggers fail on touch screens (the book notes this). Lowering commitment can just defer persuasion downstream (book's own caution [81]).

findings.summary: Niching usually wins for marginal outsiders: speak to one need, be best in a small world, create a category, avoid treading on potential partners; broaden only after the niche is saturated. Pick opportunities competitors will avoid (brand, dependency, size, track record, strengths, knowledge).
findings.limitations: Overlaps positioning skill; examples historical.

findings.summary: Visitors get distracted; be memorable and capture a way to continue the conversation (contact details, follows, retargeting), often with a low-commitment first step.
findings.limitations: Contact capture and retargeting need consent and, for retargeting, an ad budget.

findings.summary: For 'need to think about it', look for genuine reasons to act now: real deadlines with a stated reason, real scarcity, early-bird pricing. Shows travel-site notifications and checkout timers as examples; notes many firms manufacture scarcity or roll time-limited offers.
findings.limitations: Manufactured or rolling urgency and pressure notifications have since drawn regulator action in some markets; ClimbOS allows genuine urgency only.

findings.summary: Handover of Death: when the final conversion happens on a partner's page or sales team, fully persuade and qualify before handing over, get tracking on the true conversion page, be a destination people return to, give a reason to order via you, and negotiate influence over the rest of the funnel.
Conversion extends to lifetime value: deliver the best value in a niche, measure NPS (promoters 9-10 minus detractors 0-6), cross-sell after purchase, refer-a-friend, follow-up sequences.
findings.limitations: NPS validity debated; book uses it as a guiding concept.

findings.summary: goHenry case (2015 onward): research mobile visitors separately (more impulsive, less informed, more trust concerns); long mobile page addressing objections in order with repeated CTAs; Visa association made prominent; pricing page answering price and lock-in objections; activation flow and an offline letter to children tested. Reported uplifts: 78% sign-ups landing page, 191% via Facebook ads, 36% pricing page, 23% homepage, 8% and 11% activations, 470% company growth in a year.
findings.limitations: Client-reported results by the agency; no samples, intervals or test durations given. Not forecasts.

findings.summary: In regulated industries, submit ideas to compliance in small chunks with a mini business case ('micro-approvals').
Testimonials and authors' claims: 'double- and triple-digit improvements are the norm'; clients report 50-300% gains; the copyright page itself says results are unique cases, not typical.
findings.limitations: Promotional; selection of successes. Never usable as a benchmark or forecast.

findings.summary: Named tools reflect 2017-2018: Google Optimize (sunset 2023), Universal Analytics/GA360 era (replaced by GA4, 2023), Google Consumer Surveys (later Google Surveys, discontinued), Clicktale (absorbed into Contentsquare), Hotjar (later acquired by Contentsquare), Moz Fresh Web Explorer (retired), Alexa.com rankings (retired 2022), Google Checkout (retired 2013), AdWords (renamed Google Ads 2018), SurveyGizmo (renamed Alchemer), Jing, Fireworks and Macaw (discontinued), InVision (shut down), UserZoom (merged into UserTesting), Drift (now Salesloft), plus many small tag-manager and wireframing tools of uncertain status.
findings.limitations: Status per my knowledge to mid-2026; verify before naming any tool to an owner. Method categories remain valid.

findings.summary: Considered purchases carry real downside if wrong, involve research and several people; unconsidered purchases (toothpaste, lunch, gum) are low-stakes, chosen from what is in front of the buyer. Most business tech is highly considered.

Author's own toilet purchase: feature-led showroom led to three weeks and no purchase; a rep who taught three criteria (quality, aesthetics, space), eliminated options and gave an honest brand-disclosed pick closed it in 15 minutes. A consumer considered purchase, single anecdote.
findings.limitations: anecdote; consumer showroom, not B2B

findings.summary: Cites Dixon & McKenna (The JOLT Effect, 2022): 40-60% of purchase processes end in no decision, mostly from fear of a mistake rather than preference for the status quo.
findings.limitations: secondhand citation of a vendor-research book; B2B sales sample; not independently verifiable here

findings.summary: Always position against the buyer's status quo even when rival vendors are on the shortlist; part of that is making the case for change. Fear (of failure, looking stupid, being fired) is the dominant B2B emotion; trust and confidence counter it.
Cites The Challenger Sale (2011): buyers valued a rep's teaching most; buyers want help understanding options, trade-offs and pitfalls. Buyers ask 'why you over the alternatives', not 'why you'.
findings.limitations: secondhand, 2011 research

findings.summary: Buyers are experts in their pain; vendors are experts in the solution space. A first-time buyer may not know correct requirements, so pure question-led discovery leaves them overwhelmed.

Help Scout pitch: shared inbox (status quo) vs traditional help desks (cost-reduction design) -> perfect world (inbox-easy, advanced features, great experience) -> demo organised by three value points.
findings.limitations: company case as described by author

findings.summary: Qualification should precede the first call; if not, fold it into discovery. First-call demo should show your best/differentiated capabilities even unrequested; customise in a second call; skipping a demo is fine when it adds little (trial already done, databases).
Value is the answer to 'so what?'; differentiated value is value no alternative can deliver. Shared value (everyone saves time) is not a reason to buy.

Four common pitch structures each fail in sales: product walkthrough (features, no market, no discovery; ok only for educated buyers or near-identical status quo), problem/solution (competitors define the problem the same way; ok when status quo is the only rival), vision narrative (fits investors; gives buyers a reason to delay), hero's journey/StoryBrand (fits case studies; 'plan' is onboarding, no alternatives).

Origin: IBM first-call process opened with IBM's point of view on the market; applied at a start-up, revenue on path to double within months and the company was acquired. Author reports using the structure on 200+ pitches.
findings.limitations: self-reported, no comparison group

findings.summary: Structure: setup (Insight, Alternatives, Perfect World) then follow-through (Introduction, Differentiated Value, Proof, optional Objections, Ask). Goal: help the buyer understand all choices, trade-offs and when to pick you.

Weak positioning yields a weak pitch. Five components (competitive alternatives, unique capabilities, differentiated value, best-fit customers, market category) worked in that order; LevelJump worked example.

Before pitching: decide what is pitched (product vs full company for multi-product), and pitch to the champion; other stakeholders (economic buyer, end users, IT, legal/purchasing) can veto later and the champion must be armed for them.

Only position against competitors that land on shortlists; note per capability which rival lacks it; cluster value into three or fewer themes; the combination should be unique even if single themes are not. Pre-launch positioning is a thesis kept loose; review positioning a couple of times a year.

Mapping: Insight <- differentiated value + best-fit customers; Alternatives <- competitive alternatives; Perfect World <- differentiated value (purchase criteria); Introduction <- market category; Differentiated Value <- value + capabilities; Proof <- proof; Objections and Ask come from sales experience, not positioning.
Build the pitch cross-functionally (sales, marketing, product, customer success, execs) at storyboard level first; a small sales+marketing group then makes deck, demo and script.

Insight is 'the problem inside the problem': what a best-fit buyer must know to see why your unique value matters. Reverse-engineer it from differentiated value. It can be a simple statement of fact; keep it to about one slide and a minute or two; never skip it.

Group competitors into 'approaches', give pros and cons per approach for the qualified buyer, and do discovery in this step as a two-way conversation. Name competitors only if the prospect has likely seen them or they are in nearly every deal; classify rivals by your honest view but never lie. Don't introduce horizon competitors, as new options delay decisions.

Perfect World states the purchase criteria for a best-fit buyer; it ends with a check for agreement. Disagreement usually means the prospect has disqualified themselves; agreement means they have chosen your value. Setup typically 5-10 minutes.

Introduction: name the category and what the product does, briefly; for multi-product use a family diagram, for platforms a platform diagram (optionally flag optional add-ons), for infrastructure a 'marketecture' diagram showing what it replaces vs connects to.

Differentiated Value gets most of the call. Demo is organised by value theme (Value A: features; B; C), not a walkthrough. Slides-only is fine for complex infrastructure; mark what is and isn't in the base product. Table-stakes requirements (e.g. SOC 2, ERP integration) are not differentiated value; handle them as objections.

Proof can be empirical or not: case studies, third-party verification, certification, customer-validated statistics, customer quotes, analyst quotes, third-party research, awards. Your own statement isn't proof; a customer's is. Match proof to the prospect's industry, role and starting status quo.

Objections step is optional: proactively address common unspoken objections (deployment difficulty, cost, adoption, modularity, compliance/integration), especially fear of failed deployment, with specific timelines. Don't raise a common objection you can't answer well; treat it as a priority to fix.

The Ask: always end with a clear, easy-to-accept next step (POC, custom demo, trial, quote, or the sale). The first call's goal is to move good-fit buyers forward and show bad-fit buyers it isn't for them. Early-stage firms should keep the ask consistent so it can be compared.

Standardise a first-call deck and script: consistent positioning, faster rep onboarding, and the ability to measure what works. Allow improvisation that keeps the flow and value themes; recertify reps to stop drift.

Test with one respected rep on real qualified prospects; pitch builders listen and debrief each call (where lost, where excited, confusing questions); allow small wording edits only. Pass when the rep wants no more iteration and chooses it over the old pitch; fail if the best rep still prefers the old one. Failure root causes: sales not involved or weak positioning.
Pitch metrics are slow: expect more leads progressing, bad leads dropping out early, later higher close rates, better lead quality. With long cycles or low pitch volume, rely on qualitative signals.

Roll out via a recorded pitch by the test rep, practice and certification; one owner (ideally product marketing) stewards positioning and pitch; common mistakes: trend-as-insight, no discovery, too-long setup (90 s to 10 min of a 30-60 min call), weak value themes, mismatched proof, complicated ask, rolling out then forgetting.

Reuse: homepages lead with tagline + value themes and need not follow the story; explainer videos can run the full arc; buyer's guides use insight and alternatives to build categorised value/feature checklists and signal active shopping; product-led onboarding should surface differentiated value, but end-user and economic-buyer stories may differ; visuals (suite, portfolio, infrastructure fit, workflow); conference talks, research and books carry the insight, not the pitch.
Worked company pitches: LevelJump (Ch7, Ch10), Postman API-first (Ch12), Funnel marketing data hub (Ch14), Gearset compressed pitch skipping explicit pros/cons where the landscape is limited (Ch17).
findings.limitations: author-described client cases; figures (e.g. Gearset 2,000 deployments, Postman 20M users) are company claims as of ~2022-23

findings.summary: Traction means quantitative evidence of customer demand that shows in the core metric. A traction channel is any marketing or distribution route that brings real customers.
findings.limitations: Startup framing: assumes growth is the goal.

findings.summary: Founders tend to use the channels they know or that seem standard for their category. Which channel will work best is hard to predict before testing.
findings.limitations: Drawn from interviews with successful founders (survivorship).

findings.summary: Bullseye has five steps: brainstorm, rank, prioritize, test, focus. In the brainstorm, write at least one realistic idea for every channel, research how similar and failed companies acquired customers, and record guesses for each idea: likelihood of working, cost per customer, customers available before saturation, and time to test.
findings.limitations: The guesses are educated guesses that the tests are meant to replace.

findings.summary: Ranking sorts channels into most promising, possible and long-shot. The inner circle is about three channels, with the cut where enthusiasm drops off. Several are tested in parallel because tests take time to run, but too many at once causes errors from lost focus.
findings.limitations: 'About three' is the authors' heuristic, not a measured optimum.

findings.summary: Tests should be small and cheap, built for speed to data rather than traction. They answer three questions: roughly what a customer costs through the channel, how many customers it can supply, and whether they're the customers wanted now.
findings.limitations: The 'few hundred dollars' sizing is a 2014 figure.

findings.summary: Focus on the one channel that tested promising, since one channel dominates acquisition at any stage. Keep experimenting inside it until saturation or rising cost. If nothing works, repeat the process using what the tests showed (messaging, where each channel broke down).
findings.limitations: 'One channel dominates' is an author generalisation from startups.

findings.summary: Mint brainstormed, picked an inner circle (blogs, PR, search ads), ran cheap tests in each, focused on blog sponsorship and guest posts, then moved to PR when blogs maxed out. It also used a channel spreadsheet of traffic, click-through and conversion to estimate users per strategy.
findings.limitations: Self-reported by Mint's marketer; 2007 conditions.

findings.summary: The 50% rule: split time roughly evenly between product and traction, in parallel. Traction work feeds product decisions (messaging, niche, easiest customers, distribution blockers) and gives a head start at launch. The Product Trap is assuming a good product finds customers on its own.
findings.limitations: Written for founders building a new product, not owners of running businesses.

findings.summary: Dropbox tested search ads, found a customer cost well above its price, and moved to an in-product referral programme.
findings.limitations: Reported figures, not independently verified.

findings.summary: Traction work should move the needle: a measurable, meaningful change to the current goal. What counts changes by phase (first customers, then near-sustainability, then scale). Small channels can matter early and stop mattering later, and some channels (PR is the authors' example) work better later. The reach needed rises steeply: many customers at low conversion rates means reaching millions.
findings.limitations: The phases are a simplification.

findings.summary: Leaky bucket: before product-market fit, much acquisition spend leaks out, so don't scale traction spend. A steady stream of test users shows how leaky the bucket is and whether it improves.
findings.limitations: Assumes retention is the leak. It may be activation or offer.

findings.summary: Before pivoting, look for bright spots, pockets of truly engaged users, and work out why it works for them. Being slightly early to a market can be fine if early adopters exist.
findings.limitations: Based on DuckDuckGo's own story.

findings.summary: Law of Shitty Click-Throughs (quoted from Andrew Chen): marketing tactics saturate over time and response falls as they get crowded. One serious competitor in a channel raises its cost. Hence keep running small experiments and watch for new platforms while they're uncrowded.
findings.limitations: Directional. The banner-ad click-through figure is historical and unsourced.

findings.summary: Inner-circle tests validate model assumptions: cost per customer, customers available, conversion and time to acquire. Testing isn't optimisation, so a few variants are enough. Don't test until tracking exists (citing Sean Ellis); a spreadsheet is fine.
A weekly A/B test habit is claimed to improve channel efficiency 2-3x.
findings.limitations: Unsourced. Tool names are dated. Needs traffic most small businesses lack.

findings.summary: Quantify: give each channel a cost-per-customer and customer-value column so channels can be compared. Drop any channel strategy that can't plausibly deliver enough customers to move the needle within the current budget. Back-of-envelope sums matter most once many channels give some users.

Critical Path: set one traction goal tied to a significant company change (break-even, fundraise, market position). List only the milestones strictly necessary to reach it and order them by dependency. Work on the first step only and re-assess after each milestone. Set quantitative, time-bound sub-goals. Anything off the path isn't done.

Founders ignore channels for three reasons: they're out of sight, viewed negatively, or seen as tedious. Winning a channel competitors dismiss can be a (temporary) advantage. Mentors help counter bias.
findings.limitations: The advantage claim is anecdotal.

findings.summary: Viral: loop types (word of mouth, inherent, collaborative, embedded in communications, incentivised, embeds and buttons, social broadcast). Viral coefficient K is invites per user times invite conversion, with conversion split into click-through times signup. K above 1 is exponential; the authors call K above 0.5 strongly helpful. Cycle time matters as much as K. Most loops need constant seeding from other channels. Look for viral pockets by segment. Common mistakes: bolting viral features onto products that aren't inherently shareable, and too few tests.
findings.limitations: The 0.5 threshold is an author rule of thumb. Distribution platforms named are dated.

findings.summary: PR: stories filter up from small blogs and forums to big outlets, so start small. Pitch only real milestones, bundled together, with an angle that provokes emotion, and keep pitches short. Answering reporters' source requests and offering commentary are cheap starts. PR firms are costly; test it yourself first.
findings.limitations: Outlet names and platforms are dated.

findings.summary: Unconventional PR comes in two types: publicity stunts (high variance, need a deliberate ideation process) and customer appreciation (gifts, contests, great support), which is the more sustainable one.
findings.limitations: Reported stunt costs and returns are self-reported and survivorship-biased.

findings.summary: Search ads capture people actively searching, so they fit direct selling. Cost per acquisition is cost per click divided by conversion. Search ads can test messaging and product concepts before building (Archives.com landing-page tests). Don't expect early tests to profit; a campaign near break-even after a few weeks signals a channel worth focusing on. Start with a handful of ads.
findings.limitations: Platform features named (Ad Center, Conversion Optimizer, Content Network) have since changed or been renamed.

findings.summary: Average AdWords click-through is put at about 2%, with low quality scores below 1.5%, attributed to unnamed sources.
findings.limitations: Unsourced 2014 figure. Don't use as a benchmark.

findings.summary: Search ads harvest existing demand; social ads generate it and work best indirectly, by building an audience and converting it later. Put paid behind content that is already spreading organically. Buying ads directly from small relevant sites is an underused early test.
findings.limitations: The social network list and audience sizes are 2014 data.

findings.summary: Offline ads: match the medium's audience demographics to the target customer, buy remnant inventory to test cheaply, test in a local market before scaling, and track with unique URLs, codes and a 'how did you hear about us' question. Results are hard to predict and decay over time.
findings.limitations: All prices are 2014 US figures.

findings.summary: SEO: first check whether search volume could move the needle and whether ranking is realistic. Test chosen keywords with paid ads before investing. New categories may have no search demand, so target the problems and people instead. Long-tail pages can come from data the business already holds. Content and links decide rankings, and buying links breaks search guidelines.
findings.limitations: No AI search; tools named are dated. Long-tail freelance page farming carries quality risk under later search policies (our interpretation).

findings.summary: Content marketing takes months. The authors say to commit at least six months once small tests justify focus. Write about customer problems or unique own data, seed distribution by hand early, and keep a calendar.
findings.limitations: Two case studies only.

findings.summary: Email: build a permissioned list whatever channel you focus on, and never buy lists (spam). Use lifecycle emails keyed to the steps needed to reach value, retention and upsell emails, and a sender address people can reply to.
findings.limitations: Provider names are dated.

findings.summary: Engineering as marketing: free, single-purpose tools closely tied to the core product, easy to use and findable in search, treated as lasting assets. A cheap test is a small tool, or turning a popular post into a micro-site.

Targeting blogs suits the first wave of customers but has a low ceiling. Test a few small blogs representing different segments, sponsor small personal blogs, and use launch posts on link-sharing communities.
findings.limitations: The blog-discovery tools named are dated or gone.

findings.summary: BD: deals must serve the milestones that matter. Understand the partner's incentives, keep a large pipeline because most deals fail, choose partners by attributes rather than brand names, keep terms simple, and land manual deals before standardising (APIs, embeds).

Sales suits high-priced products that need hand-holding. First customers usually come from the founder's network. A good first customer has an urgent, paid problem, can actually bring change in, and works closely with you. Marketing should feed leads to sales for a repeatable model, and the funnel should remove buying friction, designed from the buyer's questions.
findings.limitations: Enterprise-centric examples.

findings.summary: Affiliate viability depends on what you can pay per customer. Paying only for defined outcomes moves risk to the affiliate. Recruit from existing customers first, and start with a simple flat or percentage payout.
findings.limitations: Network names, fees and commission rates are dated.

findings.summary: Existing platforms: go where customers already are. Rankings compound once an app gets into the charts. Fill gaps the platform leaves. Building early on a new platform gets free promotion, at the risk the platform fails.
findings.limitations: The platforms named are dated.

findings.summary: Trade shows: choose by goals, walk the show as a guest first, check the attendee fit and whether expected sales cover the cost, pre-book meetings, and put a trackable call to action on everything you hand out.
findings.limitations: The author's break-even example uses price, not margin.

findings.summary: Offline events fit when customers have no natural online gathering place or sales cycles are long. Test with a small meetup or one-day mini-conference, and check demand before selling tickets.
Speaking: test the channel by giving one talk. Organisers need speakers, credibility and lead times matter, and every talk should end with a call to action that measures interest.
Community building fits businesses whose value lies in connecting people. It needs a starting audience or seed group, a mission, cross-connections between members, and quality standards set early.
